Is Prop. 38 unconstitutional? Opponents take immunology bond fight to AG
By Tarini Mehta
Updated October 8, 2026 11:13 AM
California Attorney General Rob Bonta on Tuesday, Feb. 10, 2026, in Sacramento.
JOSÉ LUIS VILLEGAS
jvillegas@sacbee.com
The Yes on Proposition 38 campaign has raised more than $38 million and spent nearly $20 million of it on television advertisements (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=t-9WZJcETxc) in support of the $8.4 billion immunology research bond (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/election/voter-guide/article317117396.html) on the November ballot.
The No on Proposition 38 group had raised less than $640 by Sept. 19. Instead of funding ads, the group is focused on letter-writing campaigns to highlight possible issues with the ballot initiative.
On Oct. 6, they wrote a letter to California Attorney General Rob Bonta alleging that the measure may violate the state constitution.
“The stakes are substantial,” committee co-chair David Panush wrote. “Californians are being asked to assume $8.4 billion in general obligation bond debt, with half the proceeds reserved for what appears to be a single, predetermined private institution. Voters deserve to know whether this arrangement complies with the constitutional safeguards governing initiatives and the use of public funds.”
Supporters of the proposition, meanwhile, said the letter was a “campaign stunt to distract voters.”
The proposition will ask voters to allow the state to borrow $8.4 billion to support medical research in immunology and immunotherapy conducted by California research institutes and universities.
Its backers say the measure materialized as a response to the Trump administration’s cuts and freezes to thousands of research grants — many of which were later restored, but not without creating disruptions and delays. The stated goal is to allow immunology research to cure and prevent diseases like cancer and Alzheimer’s to advance unimpeded. Half of the bond proceeds would go to a single nonprofit immunology research institute affiliated with the University of California, while the rest would be distributed as competitive research grants to public or nonprofit universities and institutions.
Earlier this summer, CalMatters reported only one research institute in California (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/07/proposition-38-california/) appeared to meet the criteria for half of the immunology bond’s funds: the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy, an independent medical research organization affiliated with UCLA. Gary Michelson, a billionaire philanthropist and medical inventor, is both the co-founder of that institute and the chief backer of Prop. 38.
Last month, the opponents sent a letter to the UC Board of Regents urging them to only approve additional funding or construction commitments for the CIII if it agrees to public transparency and conflict-of-interest safeguards that public agencies are subject to. The UC board approved next steps in the construction of the institute’s facility at its September meeting.
Violation of constitution?
In a letter this week, Panush urged Bonta to weigh in on if Prop. 38 violates the California Constitution before voters decide to approve it. The attorney general is involved in the ballot initiative process in California from the very beginning. For any initiative proposed by citizens to make it onto the ballot, it must first be submitted to the attorney general with a request to prepare a title and summary that can be circulated to collect signatures — a step that was taken months ago for the immunology bond.
Suggesting Bonta take another look at the measure, Panush cited a section of the California Constitution that says an initiative that identifies a private corporation to perform any function or have any power may not be submitted to voters. While Prop. 38 does not name any private corporation, he asked if it “makes any legal difference when the requirements effectively identify it.”
For the institute that will receive half the bond proceeds if Prop. 38 passes, the measure outlined several specific requirements. The nonprofit immunology research institute must be affiliated with a University of California campus that has a hospital and clinic volume of more than 35,000 inpatient admissions and 3,500,000 outpatient visits each year. It must also own or lease a site that is at least 200,000 square feet in size and note philanthropic funding of at least $250 million in its affiliation agreement with the UC. And it must have secured $50 million to support a rapid vaccine development program and another $50 million for a microbiome research program.
“That would mean an institute connected to a health system with, say, 3 million visits, or occupying 180,000 square feet, would be excluded regardless of its research capabilities,” Panush said. “These thresholds operate as categorical exclusions, not measures of an institute’s scientific merit.”
In a previous interview with The Sacramento Bee (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article317199654.html), a spokesperson for the Yes on Proposition 38 campaign said the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy very likely meets the criteria, but the ultimate decision will be taken by the California Department of Public Health. If the state is unable to identify a suitable institute, it can modify the criteria, per the measure.
In its affiliation agreement with the UC, the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy is described as a “nonprofit public benefit corporation” governed independently of the university. First announced in 2024, the CIII is currently under construction and scheduled to open “in a year or so,” according to Yes on Proposition 38 spokesperson Robin Swanson. The institute is operational and has already administered grants, she said. A UC report indicates that construction will be complete by the end of 2028.
The UC, which sponsored a law to place a $7.5 billion scientific research bond (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article317049270.html) on the March 2028 ballot, said it does not have position on Prop. 38.
‘Saved my life’
For the supporters of the measure, the central campaign message has been that it will provide critical funding for time-sensitive immunology research. This includes finding cures for cancer, heart disease and Alzheimer’s disease.
“Prop 38 will provide much-needed funding to accelerate medical research at California’s world-class universities and research institutes, which is desperately needed in the face of federal research cuts,” Swanson said.
In a moving advertisement, cancer survivor Andrew Dale says immunotherapy saved his life and allowed him to see his daughter graduate from high school. Laurie Adami, a cancer survivor who spoke with The Bee last month, said Prop. 38 will benefit not just California (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article317199654.html), but the country and the whole world.
The measure is supported by a broad coalition of doctors, nurses and patient advocates. This includes the Alzheimer’s Association, ALS Association, the Michael J. Fox Foundation for Parkinson’s Research, American Nurses Association California, Prostate Cancer Foundation and Kidney Cancer Association. It also has the endorsement of the California Republican Party and the California Democratic Party. The Yes on Proposition 38 campaign contributed $250,000 to the Democratic Party in September.
The campaign had raised more than $38 million, as of Sept. 19, of which more than $33 million has come from billionaire philanthropist Gary Michelson and his nonprofit Michelson Center for Public Policy. Another $5 million was donated by Meyer Luskin, co-founder of the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy.
The campaign has spent nearly $20 million on cable airtime and advertisement production costs. It also spent more than $10 million earlier this year to circulate its petition and collect enough signatures to get onto the ballot.

Is Prop. 38 unconstitutional? Opponents take immunology bond fight to AG
By Tarini Mehta
Updated October 8, 2026 11:13 AM
California Attorney General Rob Bonta on Tuesday, Feb. 10, 2026, in Sacramento.
JOSÉ LUIS VILLEGAS
jvillegas@sacbee.com
The Yes on Proposition 38 campaign has raised more than $38 million and spent nearly $20 million of it on television advertisements (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=t-9WZJcETxc) in support of the $8.4 billion immunology research bond (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/election/voter-guide/article317117396.html) on the November ballot.
The No on Proposition 38 group had raised less than $640 by Sept. 19. Instead of funding ads, the group is focused on letter-writing campaigns to highlight possible issues with the ballot initiative.
On Oct. 6, they wrote a letter to California Attorney General Rob Bonta alleging that the measure may violate the state constitution.
“The stakes are substantial,” committee co-chair David Panush wrote. “Californians are being asked to assume $8.4 billion in general obligation bond debt, with half the proceeds reserved for what appears to be a single, predetermined private institution. Voters deserve to know whether this arrangement complies with the constitutional safeguards governing initiatives and the use of public funds.”
Supporters of the proposition, meanwhile, said the letter was a “campaign stunt to distract voters.”
The proposition will ask voters to allow the state to borrow $8.4 billion to support medical research in immunology and immunotherapy conducted by California research institutes and universities.
Its backers say the measure materialized as a response to the Trump administration’s cuts and freezes to thousands of research grants — many of which were later restored, but not without creating disruptions and delays. The stated goal is to allow immunology research to cure and prevent diseases like cancer and Alzheimer’s to advance unimpeded. Half of the bond proceeds would go to a single nonprofit immunology research institute affiliated with the University of California, while the rest would be distributed as competitive research grants to public or nonprofit universities and institutions.
Earlier this summer, CalMatters reported only one research institute in California (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/07/proposition-38-california/) appeared to meet the criteria for half of the immunology bond’s funds: the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy, an independent medical research organization affiliated with UCLA. Gary Michelson, a billionaire philanthropist and medical inventor, is both the co-founder of that institute and the chief backer of Prop. 38.
Last month, the opponents sent a letter to the UC Board of Regents urging them to only approve additional funding or construction commitments for the CIII if it agrees to public transparency and conflict-of-interest safeguards that public agencies are subject to. The UC board approved next steps in the construction of the institute’s facility at its September meeting.
Violation of constitution?
In a letter this week, Panush urged Bonta to weigh in on if Prop. 38 violates the California Constitution before voters decide to approve it. The attorney general is involved in the ballot initiative process in California from the very beginning. For any initiative proposed by citizens to make it onto the ballot, it must first be submitted to the attorney general with a request to prepare a title and summary that can be circulated to collect signatures — a step that was taken months ago for the immunology bond.
Suggesting Bonta take another look at the measure, Panush cited a section of the California Constitution that says an initiative that identifies a private corporation to perform any function or have any power may not be submitted to voters. While Prop. 38 does not name any private corporation, he asked if it “makes any legal difference when the requirements effectively identify it.”
For the institute that will receive half the bond proceeds if Prop. 38 passes, the measure outlined several specific requirements. The nonprofit immunology research institute must be affiliated with a University of California campus that has a hospital and clinic volume of more than 35,000 inpatient admissions and 3,500,000 outpatient visits each year. It must also own or lease a site that is at least 200,000 square feet in size and note philanthropic funding of at least $250 million in its affiliation agreement with the UC. And it must have secured $50 million to support a rapid vaccine development program and another $50 million for a microbiome research program.
“That would mean an institute connected to a health system with, say, 3 million visits, or occupying 180,000 square feet, would be excluded regardless of its research capabilities,” Panush said. “These thresholds operate as categorical exclusions, not measures of an institute’s scientific merit.”
In a previous interview with The Sacramento Bee (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article317199654.html), a spokesperson for the Yes on Proposition 38 campaign said the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy very likely meets the criteria, but the ultimate decision will be taken by the California Department of Public Health. If the state is unable to identify a suitable institute, it can modify the criteria, per the measure.
In its affiliation agreement with the UC, the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy is described as a “nonprofit public benefit corporation” governed independently of the university. First announced in 2024, the CIII is currently under construction and scheduled to open “in a year or so,” according to Yes on Proposition 38 spokesperson Robin Swanson. The institute is operational and has already administered grants, she said. A UC report indicates that construction will be complete by the end of 2028.
The UC, which sponsored a law to place a $7.5 billion scientific research bond (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article317049270.html) on the March 2028 ballot, said it does not have position on Prop. 38.
‘Saved my life’
For the supporters of the measure, the central campaign message has been that it will provide critical funding for time-sensitive immunology research. This includes finding cures for cancer, heart disease and Alzheimer’s disease.
“Prop 38 will provide much-needed funding to accelerate medical research at California’s world-class universities and research institutes, which is desperately needed in the face of federal research cuts,” Swanson said.
In a moving advertisement, cancer survivor Andrew Dale says immunotherapy saved his life and allowed him to see his daughter graduate from high school. Laurie Adami, a cancer survivor who spoke with The Bee last month, said Prop. 38 will benefit not just California (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article317199654.html), but the country and the whole world.
The measure is supported by a broad coalition of doctors, nurses and patient advocates. This includes the Alzheimer’s Association, ALS Association, the Michael J. Fox Foundation for Parkinson’s Research, American Nurses Association California, Prostate Cancer Foundation and Kidney Cancer Association. It also has the endorsement of the California Republican Party and the California Democratic Party. The Yes on Proposition 38 campaign contributed $250,000 to the Democratic Party in September.
The campaign had raised more than $38 million, as of Sept. 19, of which more than $33 million has come from billionaire philanthropist Gary Michelson and his nonprofit Michelson Center for Public Policy. Another $5 million was donated by Meyer Luskin, co-founder of the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy.
The campaign has spent nearly $20 million on cable airtime and advertisement production costs. It also spent more than $10 million earlier this year to circulate its petition and collect enough signatures to get onto the ballot.

Is Prop. 38 unconstitutional? Opponents take immunology bond fight to AG
By Tarini Mehta
Updated October 8, 2026 11:13 AM
California Attorney General Rob Bonta on Tuesday, Feb. 10, 2026, in Sacramento.
JOSÉ LUIS VILLEGAS
jvillegas@sacbee.com
The Yes on Proposition 38 campaign has raised more than $38 million and spent nearly $20 million of it on television advertisements (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=t-9WZJcETxc) in support of the $8.4 billion immunology research bond (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/election/voter-guide/article317117396.html) on the November ballot.
The No on Proposition 38 group had raised less than $640 by Sept. 19. Instead of funding ads, the group is focused on letter-writing campaigns to highlight possible issues with the ballot initiative.
On Oct. 6, they wrote a letter to California Attorney General Rob Bonta alleging that the measure may violate the state constitution.
“The stakes are substantial,” committee co-chair David Panush wrote. “Californians are being asked to assume $8.4 billion in general obligation bond debt, with half the proceeds reserved for what appears to be a single, predetermined private institution. Voters deserve to know whether this arrangement complies with the constitutional safeguards governing initiatives and the use of public funds.”
Supporters of the proposition, meanwhile, said the letter was a “campaign stunt to distract voters.”
The proposition will ask voters to allow the state to borrow $8.4 billion to support medical research in immunology and immunotherapy conducted by California research institutes and universities.
Its backers say the measure materialized as a response to the Trump administration’s cuts and freezes to thousands of research grants — many of which were later restored, but not without creating disruptions and delays. The stated goal is to allow immunology research to cure and prevent diseases like cancer and Alzheimer’s to advance unimpeded. Half of the bond proceeds would go to a single nonprofit immunology research institute affiliated with the University of California, while the rest would be distributed as competitive research grants to public or nonprofit universities and institutions.
Earlier this summer, CalMatters reported only one research institute in California (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/07/proposition-38-california/) appeared to meet the criteria for half of the immunology bond’s funds: the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy, an independent medical research organization affiliated with UCLA. Gary Michelson, a billionaire philanthropist and medical inventor, is both the co-founder of that institute and the chief backer of Prop. 38.
Last month, the opponents sent a letter to the UC Board of Regents urging them to only approve additional funding or construction commitments for the CIII if it agrees to public transparency and conflict-of-interest safeguards that public agencies are subject to. The UC board approved next steps in the construction of the institute’s facility at its September meeting.
Violation of constitution?
In a letter this week, Panush urged Bonta to weigh in on if Prop. 38 violates the California Constitution before voters decide to approve it. The attorney general is involved in the ballot initiative process in California from the very beginning. For any initiative proposed by citizens to make it onto the ballot, it must first be submitted to the attorney general with a request to prepare a title and summary that can be circulated to collect signatures — a step that was taken months ago for the immunology bond.
Suggesting Bonta take another look at the measure, Panush cited a section of the California Constitution that says an initiative that identifies a private corporation to perform any function or have any power may not be submitted to voters. While Prop. 38 does not name any private corporation, he asked if it “makes any legal difference when the requirements effectively identify it.”
For the institute that will receive half the bond proceeds if Prop. 38 passes, the measure outlined several specific requirements. The nonprofit immunology research institute must be affiliated with a University of California campus that has a hospital and clinic volume of more than 35,000 inpatient admissions and 3,500,000 outpatient visits each year. It must also own or lease a site that is at least 200,000 square feet in size and note philanthropic funding of at least $250 million in its affiliation agreement with the UC. And it must have secured $50 million to support a rapid vaccine development program and another $50 million for a microbiome research program.
“That would mean an institute connected to a health system with, say, 3 million visits, or occupying 180,000 square feet, would be excluded regardless of its research capabilities,” Panush said. “These thresholds operate as categorical exclusions, not measures of an institute’s scientific merit.”
In a previous interview with The Sacramento Bee (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article317199654.html), a spokesperson for the Yes on Proposition 38 campaign said the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy very likely meets the criteria, but the ultimate decision will be taken by the California Department of Public Health. If the state is unable to identify a suitable institute, it can modify the criteria, per the measure.
In its affiliation agreement with the UC, the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy is described as a “nonprofit public benefit corporation” governed independently of the university. First announced in 2024, the CIII is currently under construction and scheduled to open “in a year or so,” according to Yes on Proposition 38 spokesperson Robin Swanson. The institute is operational and has already administered grants, she said. A UC report indicates that construction will be complete by the end of 2028.
The UC, which sponsored a law to place a $7.5 billion scientific research bond (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article317049270.html) on the March 2028 ballot, said it does not have position on Prop. 38.
‘Saved my life’
For the supporters of the measure, the central campaign message has been that it will provide critical funding for time-sensitive immunology research. This includes finding cures for cancer, heart disease and Alzheimer’s disease.
“Prop 38 will provide much-needed funding to accelerate medical research at California’s world-class universities and research institutes, which is desperately needed in the face of federal research cuts,” Swanson said.
In a moving advertisement, cancer survivor Andrew Dale says immunotherapy saved his life and allowed him to see his daughter graduate from high school. Laurie Adami, a cancer survivor who spoke with The Bee last month, said Prop. 38 will benefit not just California (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article317199654.html), but the country and the whole world.
The measure is supported by a broad coalition of doctors, nurses and patient advocates. This includes the Alzheimer’s Association, ALS Association, the Michael J. Fox Foundation for Parkinson’s Research, American Nurses Association California, Prostate Cancer Foundation and Kidney Cancer Association. It also has the endorsement of the California Republican Party and the California Democratic Party. The Yes on Proposition 38 campaign contributed $250,000 to the Democratic Party in September.
The campaign had raised more than $38 million, as of Sept. 19, of which more than $33 million has come from billionaire philanthropist Gary Michelson and his nonprofit Michelson Center for Public Policy. Another $5 million was donated by Meyer Luskin, co-founder of the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy.
The campaign has spent nearly $20 million on cable airtime and advertisement production costs. It also spent more than $10 million earlier this year to circulate its petition and collect enough signatures to get onto the ballot.

I'm checking the Prop 14 result, which passed 51.1–48.9 in 2020, and I want the PPIC October 2020 poll figure for it. The PPIC survey I'm recalling covered Prop 15 (49% yes, 45% no), so I'm not sure it included Prop 14, and I'm looking for that number specifically.

I'm noting that the Berkeley IGS summary says no polls were available for Prop 14, so I'll check whether PPIC's October 2020 survey covered it. The No side has raised very little money, under $640 by September and about $12,000 by late October, and is relying mostly on letter-writing. Several groups and newspapers oppose it, while the Yes side has spent heavily on TV.

Prop 14 (2020) had plenty of Yes-side money and little organized opposition, yet it only squeaked by at 51%, unlike Prop 71's 59%. That suggests medical research bonds don't reliably draw overwhelming support, though the 2020 presidential-year electorate differed from a 2026 midterm, which may lean Democratic given the enthusiasm gap and Trump's low approval.

Now I'm working out the partisan breakdown: Democrats at about 70% yes, independents near 53%, Republicans around 37%, which weights to roughly 58% overall, close to the 57% topline. Next I'm thinking about how the final two weeks might shift things, with the Yes side still spending heavily on TV while the No side has almost no money and the editorial boards and HJTA are against it.

I'm weighing whether HJTA's opposition could move voters, though bond opposition from them rarely sways a majority, and their spending looks minimal at under $12,000. I'm also considering whether the billionaire framing around Michelson might make voters skeptical, while the Yes side's cancer-survivor ads probably keep them ahead. Next I want to check whether PPIC's likely-voter poll is a reliable benchmark for this.

Next I'm pulling the PPIC historical polls to see how their October numbers usually compared with final results on bonds and initiatives from 2014 to 2024, starting with the 2024 school bond.

Now I'm listing PPIC October figures against final results for several recent propositions, including the 2024 school bond, the climate bond, and the local bond threshold measure, to see how the poll numbers tended to shift.

Now I'm going through PPIC's October numbers against the final results for past propositions, with the 2020 stem cell bond still unknown, and I'm checking whether the 2020 measures on affirmative action, property tax, and gig workers moved between October and election day.

I'm now going through PPIC's October figures against final results for older propositions, checking 2018 measures like the gas tax repeal, rent control, and the dialysis initiative to see how the poll numbers tended to shift.

Now I'm going back over PPIC's October numbers for older propositions, comparing them with final results, with the 2016 and 2014 bond and tax measures next in line.

I'm estimating the chance that the measure still wins: a final result under 50% would take a drop of about seven points from the October poll, which I'd put at maybe 15–25%. The stable 55–57% support and the Yes side's large funding edge make me think it likely holds, so I'd put passage somewhere around 70–80%. The Prop 14 (2020) analog is the wrinkle I still need to settle.

Now I'm planning to check the PPIC October 2020 poll for how Prop 14 was polling before the election, to see whether a drop toward the final 51% result happened. I'll look at the PDF to find the Prop 14 figure.

PPIC STATEWIDE SURVEY: CALIFORNIANS AND THEIR GOVERNMENT
Voters Remain Divided on “Split Roll” Property Tax; Reinstating
Affirmative Action Still Trails
BIDEN HOLDS WIDE LEAD, WITH ENTHUSIASM HIGH ABOUT VOTING IN PRESIDENTIAL ELECTION
SAN FRANCISCO, October 21, 2020—With Election Day less than two weeks away, Californians remain
divided on a ballot measure that would change how commercial property is taxed. On another closely
watched ballot measure, reinstating affirmative action in the public sector has gained slightly since
September, but still has less than majority support. These are among the key findings of a statewide
survey released today by the Public Policy Institute of California.
Proposition 15 would change the tax assessment of commercial and industrial property by basing it on
current market value instead of purchase price—creating a “split roll” tax. Among likely voters, 49
percent are in favor, 45 percent oppose, and 6 percent are undecided. The margin was somewhat wider
in September (51% yes, 40% no, 9% undecided). Democrats (71%) are far more likely to say they would
vote yes than independents (42%) or Republicans (18%). Less than half of homeowners (41%) approve,
compared with 64 percent of renters. Younger Californians are more likely than older residents to
approve (60% ages 18 to 44, 42% 45 and older). Across regions, 55 percent of likely voters in Los
Angeles would vote yes, as would about half in Orange/San Diego (53%), the San Francisco Bay Area
(50%), and the Inland Empire (48%); 42 percent of likely voters in the Central Valley would vote yes.
“Californians remain closely divided on Proposition 15 as its proponents and opponents make their
closing arguments to voters over the next few weeks,” said Mark Baldassare, PPIC president and CEO.
Proposition 16 would repeal Proposition 209, a 1996 constitutional amendment that banned the use of
affirmative action involving race-based or sex-based preferences in the public sector. Among likely
voters, 37 percent would vote yes and 50 percent would vote no, with 12 percent undecided. This is a
slight gain from September, when 31 percent said yes, 47 percent said no, and 22 percent were
undecided. Today, 61 percent of Democratic likely voters support Proposition 16 (up from 46% in
September), compared with 22 percent of independents and 11 percent of Republicans (both similar to
September). Support is highest among likely voters in Los Angeles (41%) and the San Francisco Bay
Area (40%), followed by the Inland Empire (35%), Central Valley (33%), and Orange/San Diego (32%).
“Proposition 16 support has grown slightly but still falls short of a majority, with Democrats more in
favor and most Republicans and independents opposed to the measure,” Baldassare said.
Views on Confirming Barrett for Supreme Court Break along Partisan
Lines, while Majorities across Parties Oppose Overturning Roe v. Wade
Last month, President Trump nominated Judge Amy Coney Barrett to the US Supreme Court. About
four in ten Californians (41% adults, 41% likely voters) believe the Senate should confirm Barrett, while
PPIC STATEWIDE SURVEY OCTOBER 2020
PPIC.ORG/SURVEY Californians and Their Government 4
47 percent of adults and 54 percent of likely voters believe the Senate should not confirm. Views vary
widely by party affiliation, with 84 percent of Republicans, 44 percent of independents, and 16 percent
of Democrats saying the Senate should confirm.
Judge Barrett’s nomination has resurfaced the issue of whether Roe v. Wade, the landmark 1973
abortion rights ruling, could be overturned. An overwhelming majority of Californians (70%) say Roe v.
Wade should not be overturned. Across partisan groups, overwhelming majorities of Democrats (89%)
and independents (77%) and a slim majority of Republicans (53%) do not want the ruling overturned.
“Partisans are divided on the Supreme Court nominee, while majorities across party lines say that the
Supreme Court should not overturn Roe v. Wade,” Baldassare said.
Next month, the Supreme Court will hear a case challenging the constitutionality of the Affordable Care Act
(ACA), the 2010 federal health reform law. A solid majority of Californians (60%) have a favorable view of the
ACA, while a third (34%) have an unfavorable view. Across partisan groups, 88 percent of Democrats, 55
percent of independents, and 19 percent of Republicans have a favorable view.
Two in Three Are Concerned about COVID-19 Vaccine Being Rushed
A number of efforts to develop a COVID-19 vaccine are underway, with one or more vaccines possibly
available by the end of the year. Governor Newsom has announced the launch of an expert scientific
panel to independently review federally approved vaccines. Most Californians say they would definitely
(26%) or probably (31%) get the vaccine if it were available today, while a smaller share would probably
not (20%) or definitely not (20%) get the vaccine. Nationwide, a slim majority of adults say they would
definitely (21%) or probably (30%) get a vaccine if available, according to a Pew Research Center poll in
September.
At least half of Californians across party lines say they would either definitely or probably get a COVID-
19 vaccine if one were available today: 56 percent of both Democrats and independents and 50 percent
of Republicans. Across racial/ethnic groups, there are sharp differences: 70 percent of Asian Americans,
62 percent of whites, and 54 percent of Latinos say they would definitely or probably get a vaccine if
available today, with 29 percent of African Americans saying definitely or probably.
Asked about vaccine development, two-thirds of Californians (68%) are more concerned about
approval of a vaccine moving too fast, without fully ensuring safety and effectiveness, while one in four
(26%) are more concerned about approval moving too slowly, delaying access to a vaccine. Views vary
across party lines, but majorities are in agreement: 82 percent of Democrats, 73 percent of
independents, and 51 percent of Republicans are more concerned about approval moving too fast.
“One-quarter say they will definitely get the COVID-19 vaccine, with reluctance crossing party lines,
and two in three fear that approval will move too fast,” Baldassare said.
Biden Maintains Wide Lead over Trump, with Record-High Share of
Californians More Enthusiastic about Voting than Usual
As the candidates prepare for the final presidential debate tomorrow, Joe Biden maintains a sizeable
lead over Donald Trump, with 58 percent of likely voters favoring Biden/Harris and 32 percent favoring
Trump/Pence—very similar to September (60% Biden/Harris; 31% Trump/Pence). Biden leads by wide
margins in the San Francisco Bay Area (71% to 21%) and Los Angeles (70% to 22%), with narrower leads
in Orange/San Diego (50% to 37%) and the Inland Empire (48% to 42%). Trump has a narrow lead in the
Central Valley (44% to 38%).
Asked whether they are more enthusiastic or less enthusiastic than usual about voting in this
November’s presidential election, 72 percent of likely voters say they are more enthusiastic—a record
high in PPIC surveys. By comparison, four years ago in October 2016, 49 percent were more
PPIC STATEWIDE SURVEY OCTOBER 2020
PPIC.ORG/SURVEY Californians and Their Government 5
enthusiastic than usual. Majorities across party lines say they are more enthusiastic than usual this year:
79 percent of Democrats, 74 percent of Republicans, and 59 percent of independents.
“About three out of four say that they are more enthusiastic about voting in this presidential election,
with sharp increases across party lines compared to four years ago,” Baldassare said.
If the election for the US House of Representatives were held today, most likely voters (58%) would
vote for or lean toward the Democratic candidate; more than a third (37%) would vote for or lean
toward the Republican candidate. This is similar to September (60% Democratic, 33% Republican). In
the eight California House districts considered competitive according to the Cook Political Report
(districts 4, 10, 21, 22, 25, 39, 48, and 50), likely voters are divided: 49 percent favor the Republican, and
47 percent favor the Democrat. This is similar to September (54% Republican, 42% Democrat).
Californians See COVID-19 and Jobs and the Economy as Top Issues
Facing the State; Outlook for the State Is Brighter than for the US
When asked to identify the most important issue facing the state, COVID-19 (20%) and jobs and the
economy (16%) were named by more Californians than other issues. Following these are
environment/pollution/global warming (7%), homelessness (6%), housing costs/availability (6%), state
budget/deficit/spending (6%), and wildfires/fires (5%).
Amid the pandemic and a damaging wildfire season, Californians are somewhat split on whether the
state is going in the right direction or the wrong direction: 55 percent of adults and 50 percent of likely
voters say right direction, while 39 percent of adults and 46 percent of likely voters say wrong direction.
Democrats (73%) are far more likely than independents (47%) and Republicans (13%) to say right
direction. Across racial/ethnic groups, solid majorities of Asian Americans (68%), African Americans
(65%), and Latinos (60%) say right direction, while whites are divided (48% right direction, 48% wrong
direction).
In contrast to generally divided views on the state outlook, solid majorities (62% adults, 72% likely
voters) of Californians think the nation is heading in the wrong direction; 33 percent of adults and 25
percent of likely voters say the nation is heading in the right direction.
“California is facing a range of issues, including the COVID-19 and wildfire crises, at a time when
residents are much more upbeat about the direction of the state than the nation,” Baldassare said.
About Two-Thirds Think the State Is Economically Divided
Asked whether they think California is economically divided into “haves” and “have-nots,” solid
majorities of Californians (64% adults, 67% likely voters) say it is, while one in three (32% adults, 30%
likely voters) say it is not. This is consistent with the shares of adults and likely voters holding these
views in various PPIC surveys going back to 2002.
Solid majorities across income groups say the state is divided into haves and have-nots (65% annual
household income under $40,000; 63% $40,000 to under $80,000; 69% $80,000 or more). Across racial/
ethnic groups, African Americans (70%) and Latinos (68%) are most likely to hold this view, followed by
whites (61%), and Asian Americans (60%). In addition, majorities across party lines hold this view (76%
Democrats, 65% independents, 52% Republicans).
When asked which economic group they are in, 44 percent say haves and 43 percent say have-nots,
similar to November 2019 (41% haves, 44% have-nots). Today, there are wide disparities across
racial/ethnic groups in the share saying they are have-nots, with Latinos (62%) and African Americans
(53%) more likely than whites (32%) and Asian Americans (26%) to say they are have-nots.
“Two in three Californians say that we are a state of economic haves and have-nots today, with racial
disparities among those seeing themselves as have-nots,” Baldassare said.

PPIC STATEWIDE SURVEY: CALIFORNIANS AND THEIR GOVERNMENT
Voters Remain Divided on “Split Roll” Property Tax; Reinstating
Affirmative Action Still Trails
BIDEN HOLDS WIDE LEAD, WITH ENTHUSIASM HIGH ABOUT VOTING IN PRESIDENTIAL ELECTION
SAN FRANCISCO, October 21, 2020—With Election Day less than two weeks away, Californians remain
divided on a ballot measure that would change how commercial property is taxed. On another closely
watched ballot measure, reinstating affirmative action in the public sector has gained slightly since
September, but still has less than majority support. These are among the key findings of a statewide
survey released today by the Public Policy Institute of California.
Proposition 15 would change the tax assessment of commercial and industrial property by basing it on
current market value instead of purchase price—creating a “split roll” tax. Among likely voters, 49
percent are in favor, 45 percent oppose, and 6 percent are undecided. The margin was somewhat wider
in September (51% yes, 40% no, 9% undecided). Democrats (71%) are far more likely to say they would
vote yes than independents (42%) or Republicans (18%). Less than half of homeowners (41%) approve,
compared with 64 percent of renters. Younger Californians are more likely than older residents to
approve (60% ages 18 to 44, 42% 45 and older). Across regions, 55 percent of likely voters in Los
Angeles would vote yes, as would about half in Orange/San Diego (53%), the San Francisco Bay Area
(50%), and the Inland Empire (48%); 42 percent of likely voters in the Central Valley would vote yes.
“Californians remain closely divided on Proposition 15 as its proponents and opponents make their
closing arguments to voters over the next few weeks,” said Mark Baldassare, PPIC president and CEO.
Proposition 16 would repeal Proposition 209, a 1996 constitutional amendment that banned the use of
affirmative action involving race-based or sex-based preferences in the public sector. Among likely
voters, 37 percent would vote yes and 50 percent would vote no, with 12 percent undecided. This is a
slight gain from September, when 31 percent said yes, 47 percent said no, and 22 percent were
undecided. Today, 61 percent of Democratic likely voters support Proposition 16 (up from 46% in
September), compared with 22 percent of independents and 11 percent of Republicans (both similar to
September). Support is highest among likely voters in Los Angeles (41%) and the San Francisco Bay
Area (40%), followed by the Inland Empire (35%), Central Valley (33%), and Orange/San Diego (32%).
“Proposition 16 support has grown slightly but still falls short of a majority, with Democrats more in
favor and most Republicans and independents opposed to the measure,” Baldassare said.
Views on Confirming Barrett for Supreme Court Break along Partisan
Lines, while Majorities across Parties Oppose Overturning Roe v. Wade
Last month, President Trump nominated Judge Amy Coney Barrett to the US Supreme Court. About
four in ten Californians (41% adults, 41% likely voters) believe the Senate should confirm Barrett, while
PPIC STATEWIDE SURVEY OCTOBER 2020
PPIC.ORG/SURVEY Californians and Their Government 4
47 percent of adults and 54 percent of likely voters believe the Senate should not confirm. Views vary
widely by party affiliation, with 84 percent of Republicans, 44 percent of independents, and 16 percent
of Democrats saying the Senate should confirm.
Judge Barrett’s nomination has resurfaced the issue of whether Roe v. Wade, the landmark 1973
abortion rights ruling, could be overturned. An overwhelming majority of Californians (70%) say Roe v.
Wade should not be overturned. Across partisan groups, overwhelming majorities of Democrats (89%)
and independents (77%) and a slim majority of Republicans (53%) do not want the ruling overturned.
“Partisans are divided on the Supreme Court nominee, while majorities across party lines say that the
Supreme Court should not overturn Roe v. Wade,” Baldassare said.
Next month, the Supreme Court will hear a case challenging the constitutionality of the Affordable Care Act
(ACA), the 2010 federal health reform law. A solid majority of Californians (60%) have a favorable view of the
ACA, while a third (34%) have an unfavorable view. Across partisan groups, 88 percent of Democrats, 55
percent of independents, and 19 percent of Republicans have a favorable view.
Two in Three Are Concerned about COVID-19 Vaccine Being Rushed
A number of efforts to develop a COVID-19 vaccine are underway, with one or more vaccines possibly
available by the end of the year. Governor Newsom has announced the launch of an expert scientific
panel to independently review federally approved vaccines. Most Californians say they would definitely
(26%) or probably (31%) get the vaccine if it were available today, while a smaller share would probably
not (20%) or definitely not (20%) get the vaccine. Nationwide, a slim majority of adults say they would
definitely (21%) or probably (30%) get a vaccine if available, according to a Pew Research Center poll in
September.
At least half of Californians across party lines say they would either definitely or probably get a COVID-
19 vaccine if one were available today: 56 percent of both Democrats and independents and 50 percent
of Republicans. Across racial/ethnic groups, there are sharp differences: 70 percent of Asian Americans,
62 percent of whites, and 54 percent of Latinos say they would definitely or probably get a vaccine if
available today, with 29 percent of African Americans saying definitely or probably.
Asked about vaccine development, two-thirds of Californians (68%) are more concerned about
approval of a vaccine moving too fast, without fully ensuring safety and effectiveness, while one in four
(26%) are more concerned about approval moving too slowly, delaying access to a vaccine. Views vary
across party lines, but majorities are in agreement: 82 percent of Democrats, 73 percent of
independents, and 51 percent of Republicans are more concerned about approval moving too fast.
“One-quarter say they will definitely get the COVID-19 vaccine, with reluctance crossing party lines,
and two in three fear that approval will move too fast,” Baldassare said.
Biden Maintains Wide Lead over Trump, with Record-High Share of
Californians More Enthusiastic about Voting than Usual
As the candidates prepare for the final presidential debate tomorrow, Joe Biden maintains a sizeable
lead over Donald Trump, with 58 percent of likely voters favoring Biden/Harris and 32 percent favoring
Trump/Pence—very similar to September (60% Biden/Harris; 31% Trump/Pence). Biden leads by wide
margins in the San Francisco Bay Area (71% to 21%) and Los Angeles (70% to 22%), with narrower leads
in Orange/San Diego (50% to 37%) and the Inland Empire (48% to 42%). Trump has a narrow lead in the
Central Valley (44% to 38%).
Asked whether they are more enthusiastic or less enthusiastic than usual about voting in this
November’s presidential election, 72 percent of likely voters say they are more enthusiastic—a record
high in PPIC surveys. By comparison, four years ago in October 2016, 49 percent were more
PPIC STATEWIDE SURVEY OCTOBER 2020
PPIC.ORG/SURVEY Californians and Their Government 5
enthusiastic than usual. Majorities across party lines say they are more enthusiastic than usual this year:
79 percent of Democrats, 74 percent of Republicans, and 59 percent of independents.
“About three out of four say that they are more enthusiastic about voting in this presidential election,
with sharp increases across party lines compared to four years ago,” Baldassare said.
If the election for the US House of Representatives were held today, most likely voters (58%) would
vote for or lean toward the Democratic candidate; more than a third (37%) would vote for or lean
toward the Republican candidate. This is similar to September (60% Democratic, 33% Republican). In
the eight California House districts considered competitive according to the Cook Political Report
(districts 4, 10, 21, 22, 25, 39, 48, and 50), likely voters are divided: 49 percent favor the Republican, and
47 percent favor the Democrat. This is similar to September (54% Republican, 42% Democrat).
Californians See COVID-19 and Jobs and the Economy as Top Issues
Facing the State; Outlook for the State Is Brighter than for the US
When asked to identify the most important issue facing the state, COVID-19 (20%) and jobs and the
economy (16%) were named by more Californians than other issues. Following these are
environment/pollution/global warming (7%), homelessness (6%), housing costs/availability (6%), state
budget/deficit/spending (6%), and wildfires/fires (5%).
Amid the pandemic and a damaging wildfire season, Californians are somewhat split on whether the
state is going in the right direction or the wrong direction: 55 percent of adults and 50 percent of likely
voters say right direction, while 39 percent of adults and 46 percent of likely voters say wrong direction.
Democrats (73%) are far more likely than independents (47%) and Republicans (13%) to say right
direction. Across racial/ethnic groups, solid majorities of Asian Americans (68%), African Americans
(65%), and Latinos (60%) say right direction, while whites are divided (48% right direction, 48% wrong
direction).
In contrast to generally divided views on the state outlook, solid majorities (62% adults, 72% likely
voters) of Californians think the nation is heading in the wrong direction; 33 percent of adults and 25
percent of likely voters say the nation is heading in the right direction.
“California is facing a range of issues, including the COVID-19 and wildfire crises, at a time when
residents are much more upbeat about the direction of the state than the nation,” Baldassare said.
About Two-Thirds Think the State Is Economically Divided
Asked whether they think California is economically divided into “haves” and “have-nots,” solid
majorities of Californians (64% adults, 67% likely voters) say it is, while one in three (32% adults, 30%
likely voters) say it is not. This is consistent with the shares of adults and likely voters holding these
views in various PPIC surveys going back to 2002.
Solid majorities across income groups say the state is divided into haves and have-nots (65% annual
household income under $40,000; 63% $40,000 to under $80,000; 69% $80,000 or more). Across racial/
ethnic groups, African Americans (70%) and Latinos (68%) are most likely to hold this view, followed by
whites (61%), and Asian Americans (60%). In addition, majorities across party lines hold this view (76%
Democrats, 65% independents, 52% Republicans).
When asked which economic group they are in, 44 percent say haves and 43 percent say have-nots,
similar to November 2019 (41% haves, 44% have-nots). Today, there are wide disparities across
racial/ethnic groups in the share saying they are have-nots, with Latinos (62%) and African Americans
(53%) more likely than whites (32%) and Asian Americans (26%) to say they are have-nots.
“Two in three Californians say that we are a state of economic haves and have-nots today, with racial
disparities among those seeing themselves as have-nots,” Baldassare said.

Presidential Election
As the presidential race enters the final two weeks before Election Day, nearly all likely voters (92%) are
following news about the candidates very (58%) or fairly (34%) closely. Results were similar in October
2016 (60% very, 32% fairly) before the last presidential election. Today, the Democratic ticket of Joe
Biden and Kamala Harris leads over the Republican ticket of Donald Trump and Mike Pence by 26
points (58% to 32%). Findings were nearly identical in our September survey (60% to 31%). Currently,
the candidates get overwhelming support from their respective parties: 94 percent of Democrats
support Biden, and 82 percent of Republicans support Trump. Biden leads Trump among independents
(47% to 35%). Biden leads by wide margins in the San Francisco Bay Area and Los Angeles, and by
narrower margins in the Inland Empire and Orange/San Diego, while Trump holds a slight lead in the
Central Valley. Majorities of whites (55%), Latinos (57%), and those in other racial/ethnic groups (71%)
support Biden. (Sample sizes for Asian American and African American likely voters are too small for
separate analysis.) Biden’s lead over Trump is wider among women (63% to 28%) than among men
(52% to 37%), as well as among renters (62% to 21%) than among homeowners (56% to 37%) and
younger likely voters (58% to 24% 18 to 44) than among older likely voters (58% to 36% 45 and older).
He also has a wider lead among college graduates (67% to 23%) than among those with those with only
a high school diploma (45% to 36%) or some college education (54% to 39%).

of Joe Biden and Kamala Harris, the Republican ticket of Donald Trump and Mike Pence, the Libertarian
ticket of Jo Jorgensen and Spike Cohen, or the Green Party ticket of Howie Hawkins and Angela Walker?”

In contrast to generally divided views on the state outlook, solid majorities (62% adults, 72% likely
voters) of Californians think the nation is heading in the wrong direction; 33 percent of adults and 25
percent of likely voters say the nation is heading in the right direction.
“California is facing a range of issues, including the COVID-19 and wildfire crises, at a time when
residents are much more upbeat about the direction of the state than the nation,” Baldassare said.

Asked whether they think California is economically divided into “haves” and “have-nots,” solid

likely voters) say it is not. This is consistent with the shares of adults and likely voters holding these

household income under $40,000; 63% $40,000 to under $80,000; 69% $80,000 or more). Across racial/

whites (61%), and Asian Americans (60%). In addition, majorities across party lines hold this view (76%

content.thinking:
I'm checking the Prop 14 result, which passed 51.1–48.9 in 2020, and I want the PPIC October 2020 poll figure for it. The PPIC survey I'm recalling covered Prop 15 (49% yes, 45% no), so I'm not sure it included Prop 14, and I'm looking for that number specifically.

I'm noting that the Berkeley IGS summary says no polls were available for Prop 14, so I'll check whether PPIC's October 2020 survey covered it. The No side has raised very little money, under $640 by September and about $12,000 by late October, and is relying mostly on letter-writing. Several groups and newspapers oppose it, while the Yes side has spent heavily on TV.

Prop 14 (2020) had plenty of Yes-side money and little organized opposition, yet it only squeaked by at 51%, unlike Prop 71's 59%. That suggests medical research bonds don't reliably draw overwhelming support, though the 2020 presidential-year electorate differed from a 2026 midterm, which may lean Democratic given the enthusiasm gap and Trump's low approval.

Now I'm working out the partisan breakdown: Democrats at about 70% yes, independents near 53%, Republicans around 37%, which weights to roughly 58% overall, close to the 57% topline. Next I'm thinking about how the final two weeks might shift things, with the Yes side still spending heavily on TV while the No side has almost no money and the editorial boards and HJTA are against it.

I'm weighing whether HJTA's opposition could move voters, though bond opposition from them rarely sways a majority, and their spending looks minimal at under $12,000. I'm also considering whether the billionaire framing around Michelson might make voters skeptical, while the Yes side's cancer-survivor ads probably keep them ahead. Next I want to check whether PPIC's likely-voter poll is a reliable benchmark for this.

Next I'm pulling the PPIC historical polls to see how their October numbers usually compared with final results on bonds and initiatives from 2014 to 2024, starting with the 2024 school bond.

Now I'm listing PPIC October figures against final results for several recent propositions, including the 2024 school bond, the climate bond, and the local bond threshold measure, to see how the poll numbers tended to shift.

Now I'm going through PPIC's October numbers against the final results for past propositions, with the 2020 stem cell bond still unknown, and I'm checking whether the 2020 measures on affirmative action, property tax, and gig workers moved between October and election day.

I'm now going through PPIC's October figures against final results for older propositions, checking 2018 measures like the gas tax repeal, rent control, and the dialysis initiative to see how the poll numbers tended to shift.

Now I'm going back over PPIC's October numbers for older propositions, comparing them with final results, with the 2016 and 2014 bond and tax measures next in line.

I'm estimating the chance that the measure still wins: a final result under 50% would take a drop of about seven points from the October poll, which I'd put at maybe 15–25%. The stable 55–57% support and the Yes side's large funding edge make me think it likely holds, so I'd put passage somewhere around 70–80%. The Prop 14 (2020) analog is the wrinkle I still need to settle.

Now I'm planning to check the PPIC October 2020 poll for how Prop 14 was polling before the election, to see whether a drop toward the final 51% result happened. I'll look at the PDF to find the Prop 14 figure.

I'm going to check the PPIC October 2020 poll to see where Prop 14 stood before the election.

PPIC STATEWIDE SURVEY: CALIFORNIANS AND THEIR GOVERNMENT
Voters Remain Divided on “Split Roll” Property Tax; Reinstating
Affirmative Action Still Trails
BIDEN HOLDS WIDE LEAD, WITH ENTHUSIASM HIGH ABOUT VOTING IN PRESIDENTIAL ELECTION
SAN FRANCISCO, October 21, 2020—With Election Day less than two weeks away, Californians remain
divided on a ballot measure that would change how commercial property is taxed. On another closely
watched ballot measure, reinstating affirmative action in the public sector has gained slightly since
September, but still has less than majority support. These are among the key findings of a statewide
survey released today by the Public Policy Institute of California.
Proposition 15 would change the tax assessment of commercial and industrial property by basing it on
current market value instead of purchase price—creating a “split roll” tax. Among likely voters, 49
percent are in favor, 45 percent oppose, and 6 percent are undecided. The margin was somewhat wider
in September (51% yes, 40% no, 9% undecided). Democrats (71%) are far more likely to say they would
vote yes than independents (42%) or Republicans (18%). Less than half of homeowners (41%) approve,
compared with 64 percent of renters. Younger Californians are more likely than older residents to
approve (60% ages 18 to 44, 42% 45 and older). Across regions, 55 percent of likely voters in Los
Angeles would vote yes, as would about half in Orange/San Diego (53%), the San Francisco Bay Area
(50%), and the Inland Empire (48%); 42 percent of likely voters in the Central Valley would vote yes.
“Californians remain closely divided on Proposition 15 as its proponents and opponents make their
closing arguments to voters over the next few weeks,” said Mark Baldassare, PPIC president and CEO.
Proposition 16 would repeal Proposition 209, a 1996 constitutional amendment that banned the use of
affirmative action involving race-based or sex-based preferences in the public sector. Among likely
voters, 37 percent would vote yes and 50 percent would vote no, with 12 percent undecided. This is a
slight gain from September, when 31 percent said yes, 47 percent said no, and 22 percent were
undecided. Today, 61 percent of Democratic likely voters support Proposition 16 (up from 46% in
September), compared with 22 percent of independents and 11 percent of Republicans (both similar to
September). Support is highest among likely voters in Los Angeles (41%) and the San Francisco Bay
Area (40%), followed by the Inland Empire (35%), Central Valley (33%), and Orange/San Diego (32%).
“Proposition 16 support has grown slightly but still falls short of a majority, with Democrats more in
favor and most Republicans and independents opposed to the measure,” Baldassare said.
Views on Confirming Barrett for Supreme Court Break along Partisan
Lines, while Majorities across Parties Oppose Overturning Roe v. Wade
Last month, President Trump nominated Judge Amy Coney Barrett to the US Supreme Court. About
four in ten Californians (41% adults, 41% likely voters) believe the Senate should confirm Barrett, while
PPIC STATEWIDE SURVEY OCTOBER 2020
PPIC.ORG/SURVEY Californians and Their Government 4
47 percent of adults and 54 percent of likely voters believe the Senate should not confirm. Views vary
widely by party affiliation, with 84 percent of Republicans, 44 percent of independents, and 16 percent
of Democrats saying the Senate should confirm.
Judge Barrett’s nomination has resurfaced the issue of whether Roe v. Wade, the landmark 1973
abortion rights ruling, could be overturned. An overwhelming majority of Californians (70%) say Roe v.
Wade should not be overturned. Across partisan groups, overwhelming majorities of Democrats (89%)
and independents (77%) and a slim majority of Republicans (53%) do not want the ruling overturned.
“Partisans are divided on the Supreme Court nominee, while majorities across party lines say that the
Supreme Court should not overturn Roe v. Wade,” Baldassare said.
Next month, the Supreme Court will hear a case challenging the constitutionality of the Affordable Care Act
(ACA), the 2010 federal health reform law. A solid majority of Californians (60%) have a favorable view of the
ACA, while a third (34%) have an unfavorable view. Across partisan groups, 88 percent of Democrats, 55
percent of independents, and 19 percent of Republicans have a favorable view.
Two in Three Are Concerned about COVID-19 Vaccine Being Rushed
A number of efforts to develop a COVID-19 vaccine are underway, with one or more vaccines possibly
available by the end of the year. Governor Newsom has announced the launch of an expert scientific
panel to independently review federally approved vaccines. Most Californians say they would definitely
(26%) or probably (31%) get the vaccine if it were available today, while a smaller share would probably
not (20%) or definitely not (20%) get the vaccine. Nationwide, a slim majority of adults say they would
definitely (21%) or probably (30%) get a vaccine if available, according to a Pew Research Center poll in
September.
At least half of Californians across party lines say they would either definitely or probably get a COVID-
19 vaccine if one were available today: 56 percent of both Democrats and independents and 50 percent
of Republicans. Across racial/ethnic groups, there are sharp differences: 70 percent of Asian Americans,
62 percent of whites, and 54 percent of Latinos say they would definitely or probably get a vaccine if
available today, with 29 percent of African Americans saying definitely or probably.
Asked about vaccine development, two-thirds of Californians (68%) are more concerned about
approval of a vaccine moving too fast, without fully ensuring safety and effectiveness, while one in four
(26%) are more concerned about approval moving too slowly, delaying access to a vaccine. Views vary
across party lines, but majorities are in agreement: 82 percent of Democrats, 73 percent of
independents, and 51 percent of Republicans are more concerned about approval moving too fast.
“One-quarter say they will definitely get the COVID-19 vaccine, with reluctance crossing party lines,
and two in three fear that approval will move too fast,” Baldassare said.
Biden Maintains Wide Lead over Trump, with Record-High Share of
Californians More Enthusiastic about Voting than Usual
As the candidates prepare for the final presidential debate tomorrow, Joe Biden maintains a sizeable
lead over Donald Trump, with 58 percent of likely voters favoring Biden/Harris and 32 percent favoring
Trump/Pence—very similar to September (60% Biden/Harris; 31% Trump/Pence). Biden leads by wide
margins in the San Francisco Bay Area (71% to 21%) and Los Angeles (70% to 22%), with narrower leads
in Orange/San Diego (50% to 37%) and the Inland Empire (48% to 42%). Trump has a narrow lead in the
Central Valley (44% to 38%).
Asked whether they are more enthusiastic or less enthusiastic than usual about voting in this
November’s presidential election, 72 percent of likely voters say they are more enthusiastic—a record
high in PPIC surveys. By comparison, four years ago in October 2016, 49 percent were more
PPIC STATEWIDE SURVEY OCTOBER 2020
PPIC.ORG/SURVEY Californians and Their Government 5
enthusiastic than usual. Majorities across party lines say they are more enthusiastic than usual this year:
79 percent of Democrats, 74 percent of Republicans, and 59 percent of independents.
“About three out of four say that they are more enthusiastic about voting in this presidential election,
with sharp increases across party lines compared to four years ago,” Baldassare said.
If the election for the US House of Representatives were held today, most likely voters (58%) would
vote for or lean toward the Democratic candidate; more than a third (37%) would vote for or lean
toward the Republican candidate. This is similar to September (60% Democratic, 33% Republican). In
the eight California House districts considered competitive according to the Cook Political Report
(districts 4, 10, 21, 22, 25, 39, 48, and 50), likely voters are divided: 49 percent favor the Republican, and
47 percent favor the Democrat. This is similar to September (54% Republican, 42% Democrat).
Californians See COVID-19 and Jobs and the Economy as Top Issues
Facing the State; Outlook for the State Is Brighter than for the US
When asked to identify the most important issue facing the state, COVID-19 (20%) and jobs and the
economy (16%) were named by more Californians than other issues. Following these are
environment/pollution/global warming (7%), homelessness (6%), housing costs/availability (6%), state
budget/deficit/spending (6%), and wildfires/fires (5%).
Amid the pandemic and a damaging wildfire season, Californians are somewhat split on whether the
state is going in the right direction or the wrong direction: 55 percent of adults and 50 percent of likely
voters say right direction, while 39 percent of adults and 46 percent of likely voters say wrong direction.
Democrats (73%) are far more likely than independents (47%) and Republicans (13%) to say right
direction. Across racial/ethnic groups, solid majorities of Asian Americans (68%), African Americans
(65%), and Latinos (60%) say right direction, while whites are divided (48% right direction, 48% wrong
direction).
In contrast to generally divided views on the state outlook, solid majorities (62% adults, 72% likely
voters) of Californians think the nation is heading in the wrong direction; 33 percent of adults and 25
percent of likely voters say the nation is heading in the right direction.
“California is facing a range of issues, including the COVID-19 and wildfire crises, at a time when
residents are much more upbeat about the direction of the state than the nation,” Baldassare said.
About Two-Thirds Think the State Is Economically Divided
Asked whether they think California is economically divided into “haves” and “have-nots,” solid
majorities of Californians (64% adults, 67% likely voters) say it is, while one in three (32% adults, 30%
likely voters) say it is not. This is consistent with the shares of adults and likely voters holding these
views in various PPIC surveys going back to 2002.
Solid majorities across income groups say the state is divided into haves and have-nots (65% annual
household income under $40,000; 63% $40,000 to under $80,000; 69% $80,000 or more). Across racial/
ethnic groups, African Americans (70%) and Latinos (68%) are most likely to hold this view, followed by
whites (61%), and Asian Americans (60%). In addition, majorities across party lines hold this view (76%
Democrats, 65% independents, 52% Republicans).
When asked which economic group they are in, 44 percent say haves and 43 percent say have-nots,
similar to November 2019 (41% haves, 44% have-nots). Today, there are wide disparities across
racial/ethnic groups in the share saying they are have-nots, with Latinos (62%) and African Americans
(53%) more likely than whites (32%) and Asian Americans (26%) to say they are have-nots.
“Two in three Californians say that we are a state of economic haves and have-nots today, with racial
disparities among those seeing themselves as have-nots,” Baldassare said.

I've ruled out the PPIC October 2020 poll as a comparison, since its press release covered Props 15 and 16 but not Prop 14. Now I'm looking at whether PPIC has published a general analysis of how its final polls compared with results for initiatives.

I'm now recalling research on how ballot measure support tends to shift over a campaign, with "yes" shares often dropping by Election Day. I'd like to check that finding and how large the typical decline is, since this October poll's 16-point lead would need to flip to lose.

I'm estimating the chance the measure fails from its 16-point October lead, taking a 16-point swing as roughly a 5 to 15 percent risk and putting passage around 85 to 95 percent. That seems high, so I'm weighing the late-campaign shifts and how much uncertainty the final poll really carries before I settle on a number.

I'm checking whether any past California propositions that had a double-digit lead in PPIC's last poll ended up failing, and the examples I'm recalling aren't clear enough yet to count.

I'm now comparing Prop 15's slide from +11 in September to +4 in October and then its failure, which suggests a 16-point lead can erode fast when the opposition is well funded. I'm also weighing whether Prop 38's weaker opposition money makes that kind of collapse less likely here.

I'm going through a few more past California propositions with late PPIC polls, checking whether the ones that trailed or narrowly led in October ended up losing. Prop 56 and Prop 47 both sat near the outcomes I'd expect, while Prop 61 and the rent-control and gas-tax measures fell short with weaker October numbers.

I'm sizing up a few more past California propositions against their final PPIC numbers, and the record looks mixed rather than clean. For measures with a double-digit lead in the last poll, I'm estimating the failure rate at roughly 10 to 15 percent. I also want to check Prop 38, since its +16 final margin (57–41) was narrower in the September poll (55–42).

I'm reconsidering the bond angle: voters often turn against bonds when debt is the focus, and I'm recalling that the March 2020 school bond, Prop 13, failed despite majority support.

I'm trying to pin down whether Prop 13 from March 2020, a school facilities bond, actually failed, since the sources I'm recalling disagree on its vote share and on whether the 55% threshold applied. My sense is that it fell short, which would matter for how I think about bond measures in general.

I'm going back over whether Prop 13 from March 2020 actually failed, since I'm unsure whether the 55% threshold applied and what its final yes share was. I'm also thinking the PPIC note on it might be a side detail rather than something that changes the picture for this measure.

I'm weighing whether the Yes side's support erodes in the final days, since opposition spending usually drives that. Here the No side has little money, though it has earned media and newspaper endorsements, which can still matter in low-information races. Emotional Yes ads may hold up better than the more technical No critiques, and I'm checking whether party endorsements on either side change that.

I'm weighing the Republican Party's endorsement, which may not move Republican voters much. Still, the measure has broad majority support across partisan and demographic groups, which looks like a strong sign. Against that, the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association is opposing it with anti-bond messaging that could persuade conservatives, though Republicans are only about a quarter of likely voters.

I'm checking whether any lawsuit has been filed to pull Prop 38 from the ballot, since a court removal would change the answer entirely. An initiative can't be withdrawn once it qualifies, and challenges like this usually come before the ballot pamphlet is printed, so removal seems unlikely.

I'm now thinking about whether to look up Ballotpedia's page for Prop 38, which might have a polling section and more support data. I'll also check whether any late news or spending figures for the measure are worth noting.

I'm planning to check Ballotpedia's page for Prop 38, since it may list the support and opposition data I need. I also want to search for any lawsuit that could pull the measure from the ballot, and look at CalMatters' piece on the bond measures this fall to see whether it covers voter fatigue or polling.

I'm going to look up whether the bond's likelihood of passage holds up, then run the searches in parallel.

PPIC's 2020 survey didn't test Prop 14, so that comparison isn't available. Next I'll check whether anything could remove Prop 38 from the ballot, look at the CalMatters bond-measure piece for context on bond-vote patterns, and try the Ballotpedia page.
