Here’s what $44 billion would buy by Mikhail Zinshteyn (https://calmatters.org/author/mikhailzinshteyn/) October 24, 2026 Updated October 25, 2026 Republish Share this: Share on X (Opens in new window) X (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/10/bond-measures-on-california-ballot/) Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/10/bond-measures-on-california-ballot/) Share on WhatsApp (Opens in new window) WhatsApp (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/10/bond-measures-on-california-ballot/) Construction in a residential area that was burned during the Eaton Fire in 2025, in Altadena, on Aug. 3, 2026. Photo by Jules Hotz for CalMatters In summary Californians will decide on $44 billion in bonds when the vote on Propositions 1, 37 and 38. They’d take out debt to pay for housing and medical research. Follow the election results in California: Sign up for our newsletter (https://calmatters.org/subscribe-to-calmatters/california-election-newsletter/) to receive alerts when the contests for governor, Prop. 40, insurance commissioner and other key results are called. Your November ballot is welcoming you to make it rain … in bonds. You’ll see an El Nino-sized set of propositions that could flood the housing construction and science research components of the California economy with $44 billion of bond spending if the measures pass. Two of those bond proposals — Proposition 1 (https://calmatters.org/housing/homelessness/2026/10/prop-1-housing-bond/) for housing and Proposition 38 (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/10/prop-38-california/) for immunology research — are the traditional borrow-now, pay-back-later arrangements that add a few billion dollars to the overall cost of the propositions. A third, Proposition 37 (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/prop-37-explained-homeownership/), is an atypical measure that amounts to a low-risk radical experiment that taxpayers likely won’t be on the hook for, at least not directly. Historically, bond propositions win the approval of voters at higher rates than other measures. Since 2000, voters passed 23 of the 26 statewide bonds before them, an 88% yay rate. In recent years voters approved billions in bond debt for school construction, combatting the effects of climate change and housing for veterans. Bonds are a form of debt that the state must pay off over time, and that means annual payments with interest (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/voter-info/overview-state-bond-debt.htm). The state spends $6 billion annually to repay about $80 billion of bonds. Voters and lawmakers have also approved $40 billion in bonds that have yet to be sold. Fortunately for your ballot studying, the following cheat sheet is a primer on just the three bonds before you. Prop. 1: Affordable housing If voters say yes, Prop. 1 would permit California’s treasurer (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-1-housing-bond/) to sell $11.25 billion in general obligation bonds. That money would provide various types of housing, including to veterans, homeless Californians, renters, homeowners, farmworkers, students and tribes. The measure dedicates $7 billion to constructing, refurbishing, or acquiring apartment complexes, primarily through loans to developers of affordable housing. These developments must serve low-income residents, reserving at least 10% of units for extremely low-income households. Over $1 billion of this total supports permanent and interim housing for the homeless. The bond, if passed, would result in some 40,000 new rental units, wrote (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop1-110326.pdf) the Legislative Analyst’s Office, which is the nonpartisan think-tank of the Legislature. This is the only bond measure on the ballot put forward by lawmakers. The other two secured enough signatures from voters to secure a spot for the November election. Opposition to this bond is minimal. The state Republican Party’s officially neutral on the measure. Several Republican lawmakers in June voted no on the bill that metamorphosed into this bond. They argued that the bill’s title — The Veterans and Affordable Housing Bond Act (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/bills/ca_202520260sb417) — misled the public on just how much of the bond revenue would support veterans. The answer? $1.25 billion for veterans to secure home loans. Another $350 million would head to the state’s two public university systems to help finance the development of student dorms. But with costs per bed often exceeding $250,000, all those tens of millions of dollars would secure dorms for around 1,300 students. Just the right amount of news Just the right amount of news Get California’s most essential headlines without feeling overwhelmed. Get California’s most essential headlines without feeling overwhelmed. Email address By clicking subscribe, you agree to the terms (https://calmatters.org/about/policies-and-standards/). Sign up for free Δ Support for Prop. 1 is vast, including Gov. Gavin Newsom, the state Democratic party, home-sharing company AirBnB, major unions and more. Want more? Read CalMatters’ Marisa Kendall’s guide to Prop. 1 (https://calmatters.org/housing/homelessness/2026/10/prop-1-housing-bond/). Prop. 37: Help for down payments This bond measure is strange (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-37-homebuyers-loan/), novel and introduces a bevy of unknowns. Confused? So is everyone else, which is why CalMatters’ housing reporter Ben Christopher described this unorthodox proposition as “plainly weird.” (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/prop-37-explained-homeownership/) Prop. 37 should be viewed as a way to help buyers of new homes secure down payments. The language permits individuals to apply for as much as 17% of the purchase price of a new house, condo or townhome. That covers much of the typical 20% down payment. Who’s eligible? Roughly 90% of all California renters. The income caps vary by county, so around $115,000 in Imperial and north of $400,000 in San Mateo for a family of three. Eligible homes must satisfy several conditions: They’re new or newly converted and don’t cost more than roughly $1.5 million in the Bay Area or $1 million in Riverside — again, it’s based on a weedy formula by county. What won’t it do? Add to the state’s debt repayment log. This is not a bond that taxpayers will pay back; instead private lenders who provide this bond money will be repaid by homebuyers in the form of interest payments. How many homes this could buy is impossible to predict. That number depends on how much the new homes cost, the incomes of the homebuyers and whether developers build new homes. Most renters today couldn’t afford even the cheapest new homes, said Eric McGhee, an analyst for the nonprofit Public Policy Institute of California who’s written about Prop. 37 (https://www.ppic.org/blog/how-many-might-actually-use-the-down-payment-assistance-in-proposition-37/). He estimated that anywhere from 60,000 to more than 1.8 million buyers could take advantage of the down payment assistance through this bond measure. The lower end assumes a 20% down payment on the most expensive homes. The higher end assumes 5% down payments on the least expensive homes. Prop. 38: Immunology research This bond proposal (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-38-research-bond/) would commit $4.2 billion to a single, unnamed nonprofit institute that focuses on immunology research and cures for major diseases such as Alzheimer’s, cancer and heart disease. The same amount would be distributed to a committee that’d identify a limited number of researchers at public universities and nonprofits who study immunology and immunotherapies. Previous reporting by CalMatters (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/07/proposition-38-california/) found only one institute in California currently meets Prop. 38’s criteria for half of the money: the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy. The institute’s primary funder is billionaire Gary K. Michelson, who wrote Prop. 38 and is by far the largest donor to its political campaign. Additional CalMatters reporting raises the question of how ready is the institute to implement the bond’s vast dollars. The institute had only three employees (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/10/prop-38-california/) as of last month, far fewer than the 51 it planned to have on staff last year. The Yes on 38 campaign says the bond revenue is needed to hedge against the Trump administration’s ongoing efforts to cut federal science research or limit what’s studied. They argue that any curtailment of drug trials and other therapies can lead to avoidable pain and death for patients of debilitating maladies. Opponents of the measure fault it for concentrating half the money in a single institute and limiting which other researchers can receive the funding. They say science research is best performed in a competitive environment that’s open to all of California’s nonprofit and public university scientists. # Group challenges constitutionality of $8.4B proposition
Mon, October 19, 2026 by The Center Square
(The Center Square) – A group opposing Proposition 38, a ballot measure in California’s Nov. 3 election, is challenging the constitutionality of the $8.4 billion measure.
The proposition would use all of that funding to pay for immunology research, all backed by general obligation bond funds paid for by California’s taxpayers.
Roughly half of that $8.4 billion could go to one institution – the California Institute of Immunology and Immunotherapy at University of California, Los Angeles, opponents of the measure told The Center Square.
Those opponents are questioning how legal that is.
Part of the problem is the criteria are so specific only one or two institutions can qualify for the money, opponents of Prop.
38 told The Center Square.
“They created these criteria to be eligible to compete, and that eligibility is predicated almost entirely on UCLA’s numbers,” Robert Kaplan, co-chair of the No on Prop.
38 campaign, told The Center Square.
“So you’d have to have more than 3.5 million outpatient visits per year, and UCLA has a little bit more than that.
UCSF [University of California, San Francisco] is 3.4 [million].”
According to the proposition, the bond money could only go to an institution affiliated with the University of California, the state’s 10-campus public university system.

# Is Prop. 38 unconstitutional? Opponents take immunology bond fight to AG
...
The Yes on Proposition 38 campaign has raised more than $38 million and spent nearly $20 million of it on television advertisements in support of the $8.4 billion immunology research bond on the November ballot.
The No on Proposition 38 group had raised less than $640 by Sept. 19. Instead of funding ads, the group is focused on letter-writing campaigns to highlight possible issues with the ballot initiative.
On Oct. 6, they wrote a letter to California Attorney General Rob Bonta alleging that the measure may violate the state constitution.

Photo by Jules Hotz for CalMatters In summary Californians will decide on $44 billion in bonds when the vote on Propositions 1, 37 and 38. They’d take out debt to pay for housing and medical research. Follow the election results in California: Sign up for our newsletter (https://calmatters.org/subscribe-to-calmatters/california-election-newsletter/) to receive alerts when the contests for governor, Prop. 40, insurance commissioner and other key results are called. Your November ballot is welcoming you to make it rain … in bonds. You’ll see an El Nino-sized set of propositions that could flood the housing construction and science research components of the California economy with $44 billion of bond spending if the measures pass. Two of those bond proposals — Proposition 1 (https://calmatters.org/housing/homelessness/2026/10/prop-1-housing-bond/) for housing and Proposition 38 (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/10/prop-38-california/) for immunology research — are the traditional borrow-now, pay-back-later arrangements that add a few billion dollars to the overall cost of the propositions. A third, Proposition 37 (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/prop-37-explained-homeownership/), is an atypical measure that amounts to a low-risk radical experiment that taxpayers likely won’t be on the hook for, at least not directly. Historically, bond propositions win the approval of voters at higher rates than other measures. Since 2000, voters passed 23 of the 26 statewide bonds before them, an 88% yay rate. In recent years voters approved billions in bond debt for school construction, combatting the effects of climate change and housing for veterans. Bonds are a form of debt that the state must pay off over time, and that means annual payments with interest (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/voter-info/overview-state-bond-debt.htm). The state spends $6 billion annually to repay about $80 billion of bonds. Voters and lawmakers have also approved $40 billion in bonds that have yet to be sold. Fortunately for your ballot studying, the following cheat sheet is a primer on just the three bonds before you. Prop. 1: Affordable housing If voters say yes, Prop. 1 would permit California’s treasurer (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-1-housing-bond/) to sell $11.25 billion in general obligation bonds. That money would provide various types of housing, including to veterans, homeless Californians, renters, homeowners, farmworkers, students and tribes. The measure dedicates $7 billion to constructing, refurbishing, or acquiring apartment complexes, primarily through loans to developers of affordable housing. These developments must serve low-income residents, reserving at least 10% of units for extremely low-income households. Over $1 billion of this total supports permanent and interim housing for the homeless. The bond, if passed, would result in some 40,000 new rental units, wrote (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop1-110326.pdf) the Legislative Analyst’s Office, which is the nonpartisan think-tank of the Legislature. This is the only bond measure on the ballot put forward by lawmakers. The other two secured enough signatures from voters to secure a spot for the November election. I've ruled out the PPIC October 2020 poll as a comparison, since its press release covered Props 15 and 16 but not Prop 14. Now I'm looking at whether PPIC has published a general analysis of how its final polls compared with results for initiatives.

I'm now recalling research on how ballot measure support tends to shift over a campaign, with "yes" shares often dropping by Election Day. I'd like to check that finding and how large the typical decline is, since this October poll's 16-point lead would need to flip to lose.

I'm estimating the chance the measure fails from its 16-point October lead, taking a 16-point swing as roughly a 5 to 15 percent risk and putting passage around 85 to 95 percent. That seems high, so I'm weighing the late-campaign shifts and how much uncertainty the final poll really carries before I settle on a number.

I'm checking whether any past California propositions that had a double-digit lead in PPIC's last poll ended up failing, and the examples I'm recalling aren't clear enough yet to count.

I'm now comparing Prop 15's slide from +11 in September to +4 in October and then its failure, which suggests a 16-point lead can erode fast when the opposition is well funded. I'm also weighing whether Prop 38's weaker opposition money makes that kind of collapse less likely here.

I'm going through a few more past California propositions with late PPIC polls, checking whether the ones that trailed or narrowly led in October ended up losing. Prop 56 and Prop 47 both sat near the outcomes I'd expect, while Prop 61 and the rent-control and gas-tax measures fell short with weaker October numbers.

I'm sizing up a few more past California propositions against their final PPIC numbers, and the record looks mixed rather than clean. For measures with a double-digit lead in the last poll, I'm estimating the failure rate at roughly 10 to 15 percent. I also want to check Prop 38, since its +16 final margin (57–41) was narrower in the September poll (55–42).

I'm reconsidering the bond angle: voters often turn against bonds when debt is the focus, and I'm recalling that the March 2020 school bond, Prop 13, failed despite majority support.

I'm trying to pin down whether Prop 13 from March 2020, a school facilities bond, actually failed, since the sources I'm recalling disagree on its vote share and on whether the 55% threshold applied. My sense is that it fell short, which would matter for how I think about bond measures in general.

I'm going back over whether Prop 13 from March 2020 actually failed, since I'm unsure whether the 55% threshold applied and what its final yes share was. I'm also thinking the PPIC note on it might be a side detail rather than something that changes the picture for this measure.

I'm weighing whether the Yes side's support erodes in the final days, since opposition spending usually drives that. Here the No side has little money, though it has earned media and newspaper endorsements, which can still matter in low-information races. Emotional Yes ads may hold up better than the more technical No critiques, and I'm checking whether party endorsements on either side change that.

I'm weighing the Republican Party's endorsement, which may not move Republican voters much. Still, the measure has broad majority support across partisan and demographic groups, which looks like a strong sign. Against that, the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association is opposing it with anti-bond messaging that could persuade conservatives, though Republicans are only about a quarter of likely voters.

I'm checking whether any lawsuit has been filed to pull Prop 38 from the ballot, since a court removal would change the answer entirely. An initiative can't be withdrawn once it qualifies, and challenges like this usually come before the ballot pamphlet is printed, so removal seems unlikely.

Photo by Jules Hotz for CalMatters In summary Californians will decide on $44 billion in bonds when the vote on Propositions 1, 37 and 38. They’d take out debt to pay for housing and medical research. Follow the election results in California: Sign up for our newsletter (https://calmatters.org/subscribe-to-calmatters/california-election-newsletter/) to receive alerts when the contests for governor, Prop. 40, insurance commissioner and other key results are called. Your November ballot is welcoming you to make it rain … in bonds. You’ll see an El Nino-sized set of propositions that could flood the housing construction and science research components of the California economy with $44 billion of bond spending if the measures pass. Two of those bond proposals — Proposition 1 (https://calmatters.org/housing/homelessness/2026/10/prop-1-housing-bond/) for housing and Proposition 38 (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/10/prop-38-california/) for immunology research — are the traditional borrow-now, pay-back-later arrangements that add a few billion dollars to the overall cost of the propositions. A third, Proposition 37 (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/prop-37-explained-homeownership/), is an atypical measure that amounts to a low-risk radical experiment that taxpayers likely won’t be on the hook for, at least not directly. Historically, bond propositions win the approval of voters at higher rates than other measures. Since 2000, voters passed 23 of the 26 statewide bonds before them, an 88% yay rate. In recent years voters approved billions in bond debt for school construction, combatting the effects of climate change and housing for veterans. Bonds are a form of debt that the state must pay off over time, and that means annual payments with interest (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/voter-info/overview-state-bond-debt.htm). The state spends $6 billion annually to repay about $80 billion of bonds. Voters and lawmakers have also approved $40 billion in bonds that have yet to be sold. Fortunately for your ballot studying, the following cheat sheet is a primer on just the three bonds before you. Prop. 1: Affordable housing If voters say yes, Prop. 1 would permit California’s treasurer (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-1-housing-bond/) to sell $11.25 billion in general obligation bonds. That money would provide various types of housing, including to veterans, homeless Californians, renters, homeowners, farmworkers, students and tribes. The measure dedicates $7 billion to constructing, refurbishing, or acquiring apartment complexes, primarily through loans to developers of affordable housing. These developments must serve low-income residents, reserving at least 10% of units for extremely low-income households. Over $1 billion of this total supports permanent and interim housing for the homeless. The bond, if passed, would result in some 40,000 new rental units, wrote (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop1-110326.pdf) the Legislative Analyst’s Office, which is the nonpartisan think-tank of the Legislature. This is the only bond measure on the ballot put forward by lawmakers. The other two secured enough signatures from voters to secure a spot for the November election. Opposition to this bond is minimal. The state Republican Party’s officially neutral on the measure. Several Republican lawmakers in June voted no on the bill that metamorphosed into this bond. They argued that the bill’s title — The Veterans and Affordable Housing Bond Act (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/bills/ca_202520260sb417) — misled the public on just how much of the bond revenue would support veterans. The answer? $1.25 billion for veterans to secure home loans. Another $350 million would head to the state’s two public university systems to help finance the development of student dorms. But with costs per bed often exceeding $250,000, all those tens of millions of dollars would secure dorms for around 1,300 students. Just the right amount of news Just the right amount of news Get California’s most essential headlines without feeling overwhelmed. Get California’s most essential headlines without feeling overwhelmed. Email address By clicking subscribe, you agree to the terms (https://calmatters.org/about/policies-and-standards/). Sign up for free Δ Support for Prop. 1 is vast, including Gov. Gavin Newsom, the state Democratic party, home-sharing company AirBnB, major unions and more. Want more? Read CalMatters’ Marisa Kendall’s guide to Prop. 1 (https://calmatters.org/housing/homelessness/2026/10/prop-1-housing-bond/). Prop. 37: Help for down payments This bond measure is strange (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-37-homebuyers-loan/), novel and introduces a bevy of unknowns. Confused? So is everyone else, which is why CalMatters’ housing reporter Ben Christopher described this unorthodox proposition as “plainly weird.” (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/prop-37-explained-homeownership/) Prop. 37 should be viewed as a way to help buyers of new homes secure down payments. The language permits individuals to apply for as much as 17% of the purchase price of a new house, condo or townhome. That covers much of the typical 20% down payment. Who’s eligible? Roughly 90% of all California renters. The income caps vary by county, so around $115,000 in Imperial and north of $400,000 in San Mateo for a family of three. Eligible homes must satisfy several conditions: They’re new or newly converted and don’t cost more than roughly $1.5 million in the Bay Area or $1 million in Riverside — again, it’s based on a weedy formula by county. What won’t it do? Add to the state’s debt repayment log. This is not a bond that taxpayers will pay back; instead private lenders who provide this bond money will be repaid by homebuyers in the form of interest payments. How many homes this could buy is impossible to predict. That number depends on how much the new homes cost, the incomes of the homebuyers and whether developers build new homes. Most renters today couldn’t afford even the cheapest new homes, said Eric McGhee, an analyst for the nonprofit Public Policy Institute of California who’s written about Prop. 37 (https://www.ppic.org/blog/how-many-might-actually-use-the-down-payment-assistance-in-proposition-37/). He estimated that anywhere from 60,000 to more than 1.8 million buyers could take advantage of the down payment assistance through this bond measure. The lower end assumes a 20% down payment on the most expensive homes. The higher end assumes 5% down payments on the least expensive homes. Prop. 38: Immunology research This bond proposal (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-38-research-bond/) would commit $4.2 billion to a single, unnamed nonprofit institute that focuses on immunology research and cures for major diseases such as Alzheimer’s, cancer and heart disease. The same amount would be distributed to a committee that’d identify a limited number of researchers at public universities and nonprofits who study immunology and immunotherapies. Previous reporting by CalMatters (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/07/proposition-38-california/) found only one institute in California currently meets Prop. 38’s criteria for half of the money: the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy. The institute’s primary funder is billionaire Gary K. Michelson, who wrote Prop. 38 and is by far the largest donor to its political campaign. Additional CalMatters reporting raises the question of how ready is the institute to implement the bond’s vast dollars. The institute had only three employees (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/10/prop-38-california/) as of last month, far fewer than the 51 it planned to have on staff last year. The Yes on 38 campaign says the bond revenue is needed to hedge against the Trump administration’s ongoing efforts to cut federal science research or limit what’s studied. They argue that any curtailment of drug trials and other therapies can lead to avoidable pain and death for patients of debilitating maladies. Opponents of the measure fault it for concentrating half the money in a single institute and limiting which other researchers can receive the funding. They say science research is best performed in a competitive environment that’s open to all of California’s nonprofit and public university scientists. How this is built
Proposition 38 is forecast as a bonds and budgets measure whose Yes vote leans to neither party . Comparable measures from 2018 to 2024 set how far its Yes share moves with California 's partisanship, and each county moves with its own age, education, race and density mix as well as its 2024 presidential vote, so no two counties share a margin by default. How it reached the ballot moves it further. I'm noting that the On Point Politics forecast gives Proposition 38 a 94.8% chance of passing, based on polls with adjustments. Since it's a forecasting site with a fairly simple model, I don't want to weigh that number too heavily.

I'm going to check the methodology page to see how the forecast turns polling into that 94.8% figure, since it notes the undecided voters split two to one for No. I'll treat the number as a rough estimate for now. The PPIC September poll also had Yes at 55-42, or 56.0% after adjustment, and the Politico report shows Yes campaign spending far outpacing No.

I'm going to check the On Point Politics methodology for how they handle historical polling error, since a calibrated error range would tell me how much the 94.8% figure can really bear. On the No side, the spending gap is so large that a late push would be hard to match, though big campaigns have overcome money gaps before. The one open question is whether PPIC's likely voter sample leans too young and enthusiastic, given older voters were less supportive in September.

I'm weighing the poll-based estimate of roughly 75–85% for Yes. Young voters favor it strongly, and the billionaire-funding angle might hurt the Yes side among some voters, but Democratic endorsement still keeps Democratic support around 70%. That points toward Yes being the likelier winner.

I'm weighing whether the question means "Is the Yes side more likely to win?" or asks something else about the sides. Given the forecast and polling, the answer I'm leaning toward is "yes," since the Yes side appears favored.

Yes side confirmed as likely winner on both readings of the question. Next I'll check the On Point Politics methodology and look for late-breaking news, like the reported $120 million pledge from Michelson, which would mean the Yes side still has more money for a final push.

Comparable measures from 2018 to 2024 set how far its Yes share moves with California 's partisanship, and each county moves with its own age, education, race and density mix as well as its 2024 presidential vote, so no two counties share a margin by default. How it reached the ballot moves it further. Polls then pull the forecast toward them by recency and size, after splitting undecided voters two to one for No. Sources: elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/ccrov/2026/june/26179jj.pdf), growsf.org (https://growsf.org/news/2026-07-02-14-state-measures/), ppic.org (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/). The search results show Prop 42's AP page still at "0% of votes counted," with polls not yet closed, so the election hasn't happened as of the latest data. The ABC7 live updates page was last updated on November 3, 2026, at 4:37 AM Pacific, so I'm working out what the current date probably is.

I'm looking for the Ballotpedia details next, since their fetch came back empty. The polling leans yes, with Democrats strongly in favor and Republicans split against it, and the yes campaign has far outspent the no side.

I'm checking the SacBee endorsements for Prop 38, and I'm noting the main opponents: the League of Women Voters, Common Cause, and a Stanford professor. Next I'm weighing how reliable a 57% final PPIC reading is, using past California initiatives that polled similarly and either passed or failed.

I'm weighing whether a 57% yes in the final PPIC poll is safe. Undecideds are only 2 to 3 percent, but initiatives often lose several points of support as a campaign goes on, which could push this one close to even.

I'm checking how past California bond measures held up against their final polls, since bonds often hold their support. The 2024 school and climate bonds seem to have gained a little, while Prop 1 and Prop 5 slipped, so the pattern is mixed.

I'm comparing how PPIC's late-October numbers for past propositions held up against the final results, to see whether a 57% yes reading usually survives. The most striking case is Prop 27 in 2022, where support dropped sharply by election day, which suggests a close outcome here is possible.

I'm comparing these past propositions' late-October polls with their final results, and the spread is wide, though PPIC's numbers usually land within about five points of the final yes share. For Prop 38 at 57%, that suggests a finish somewhere around 50 to 58%, which I'd put at roughly a 65 to 75% chance of passing. The main thing pulling it down is that the no side has almost no money, while the yes side has about $71 million to spend.

I'm weighing how the heavy funding gap and the lack of organized opposition might keep the yes side's support from eroding. I'm also noting that the two housing bonds already on the ballot are polling above 60%, which may not matter much here, and that Republican support sits at only 37% even after the party's endorsement.

The partisan split holds up: Republicans at 37% yes is low, but the GOP endorsement suggests the measure isn't seen as a purely partisan fight. Older voters leaning no in September matter, since midterm electorates skew older, and I'm weighing whether the likely-voter weighting already accounts for that.

I'm checking whether any major opposition money, perhaps from the pharmaceutical industry, is behind the No side, and the SOS filings show only about $12,000 raised for "No on Proposition 38." That points to a weak opposition campaign, though I want to confirm there are no unlisted independent committees.

I'm going to check whether any other pollsters, like Emerson, Berkeley IGS, or SurveyUSA, tested Prop 38 in late October, and I'll also look for the Yes campaign's ad spending and what the No side is saying, including who's backing it.

I'm now looking for the McClatchy endorsement list, including the Sacramento Bee's position on Prop 38, along with the LA Times and SF Chronicle editorials. Editorial endorsements likely move voters only a little, but with a strongly negative editorial consensus and a big money gap, I'm still considering that the measure could pass.

I'm looking for analyses of how support for ballot measures tends to shift as elections approach, from Ballotpedia or the Field Poll. I'm also noting that Gary Michelson and Meyer Luskin sponsored Prop 38 and put in roughly $40 million or more, which typically helps the yes side hold its numbers.

I'm going to pull up the PPIC report itself to check the 57% yes figure and whether it differs once respondents have read the ballot label.

Key Findings
Mail ballots have been sent to all California voters and the November 3 general election is in its final days. Californians are being asked to choose their next governor as well as other state constitutional officers and state legislators; they are also making important policy decisions through 14 state propositions. In addition, the 2026 California midterm ballot features 52 US House races; with a closely divided Congress, a few of these races may help to determine which party controls the 120th Congress. The economy is top of mind, with recent trends in inflation, consumer spending, interest rates, and jobs sending mixed signals.
These are the key findings of the Californians and their Government survey—which includes questions on topics including the November governor’s race, House races, five legislative ballot measures, nine citizens’ initiatives, state issues, and national issues—that was conducted from October 16–October 22, 2026:
Xavier Becerra (D) leads Steve Hilton (R) by a 24 point margin (61% to 37%) in the governor’s race. Democratic candidates lead Republican candidates in local House district races by a 28 point margin (63% to 35%). Overwhelming majorities of partisans support their party’s candidates while independents favor the Democratic candidates. Sixty percent are satisfied with the choice of gubernatorial candidates. Sixty-six percent are closely following news about the governor’s race. Fifty-eight percent are more enthusiastic about voting than usual for Congress this year. Majorities say that they would vote yes on Proposition 1 (60%; Housing Bond) and Proposition 2 (61%; Rainy Day Fund), with partisans varying in support; three legislative ballot measures falls short of a majority.
Forty-six percent would vote yes on Proposition 40 (Imposes One-Time Tax) after reading the ballot title and label. Majorities would vote yes on Proposition 3 (58%; Extending Tax on High Incomes), Proposition 37 (65%; Loan Program for Middle-Income Home Buyers), Proposition 38 (57%; Immunology Bond), and Proposition 42 (51%; Prohibits New State Property Taxes). Support varies across partisan groups, and support for five citizens’ initiatives fall short of a majority. Most say the state’s voter information guide is at least “somewhat” useful in deciding how to vote on citizens’ initiatives and report that they are at least “somewhat” satisfied with the information about the citizens’ initiatives.
Half of Californians choose cost of living, inflation, and the economy as well as housing costs and availability as the most important issues facing California today. Majorities of adults and likely voters think the state is headed in the wrong direction, and overwhelming majorities expect the state to have bad times financially in the next 12 months. Forty-seven percent of adults and 49 percent of likely voters say they approve of Governor Gavin Newsom’s job performance. Majorities of adults and likely voters say their incomes are not keeping up with inflation and that housing affordability is a big problem in their part of California. Sixty-three percent of likely voters have a great deal or quite a lot of confidence in the system in which votes are cast and counted in California.
Almost half of Californians name economic conditions and threats to democratic values and norms as the most important problems facing the nation today. Overwhelming majorities of adults and likely voters think the nation is generally going in the wrong direction and expect the nation to have bad times financially in the next 12 months. Twenty-one percent of adults and 26 percent of likely voters say they approve of President Donald Trump’s job performance. About one in four adults and likely voters approve of the job that US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) is doing, and a similar share approve of US military action against Iran. About three in ten are very satisfied or somewhat satisfied with the way US democracy is working. Sixty-five percent of likely voters are very confident or somewhat confident that the votes for Congress across the country will be accurately cast and counted in this year’s election.
November Races and Legislative Ballot Measures
Ballots and voter guides for the November 3 election have been mailed to California’s registered voters. At the top of the ticket is the governor’s race, with voters deciding who will replace Gavin Newsom. The 52 House races in California will help to determine the party in control of a closely divided US Congress. Voters will be the deciders on 14 state propositions—five legislative ballot measures and nine citizens’ initiatives—including several tax proposals, multibillion-dollar bonds, and election reforms. Voter engagement is a crucial factor in turnout for this midterm election.
Gubernatorial Election. California likely voters say they would choose Xavier Becerra (D) over Steve Hilton (R) by a 24 point margin (61% to 37%) if the November 3 election for governor were held today. Becerra led Hilton by 22 points in our September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/) (60% to 38%) and by 25 points in our July survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-the-environment-july-2026/) (61% to 36%). Today, partisans overwhelmingly support their party’s gubernatorial candidate: 92 percent of Democrats support Becerra, and 89 percent of Republicans favor Hilton. Most independent likely voters favor the Democratic candidate for governor (54% Becerra, 41% Hilton), and half or more of likely voters favor Becerra over Hilton across demographic groups and the state’s major regions.
Sixty percent of likely voters say that they are satisfied with their choices of gubernatorial candidates in the November 3 election, while 39 percent are not satisfied. Shares expressing satisfaction with the gubernatorial candidate choices were similar before the June primary (62% May survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/)), the 2022 general election (62% October 2022 survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2022/) ) , and the 2018 general election (60% October 2018 survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2018/)). Today, majorities of Democrats (65%) and Republicans (67%) are satisfied, compared to fewer than half of independents (44%). Majorities of Becerra supporters (63%) and Hilton supporters (59%) are satisfied with the gubernatorial candidate choices. Half or more across demographic groups and the state’s major regions are satisfied; notably, satisfaction varies by age (50% 18 to 34; 52% 35 to 54; 69% 55 and older).
About two in three likely voters are closely following news about candidates for the governor’s election (22% very, 44% fairly). In our May survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) before the June primary, about seven in ten were closely following news about candidates in the governor’s election (23% very, 48% fairly). By comparison, about six in ten were closely following news about the candidates in the gubernatorial election in October 2022 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2022/) (25% very, 35% fairly) and in October 2018 (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-likely-voters-1018.pdf) (21% very, 41% fairly). Today, majorities across partisan groups (69% Democrats, 70% Republicans, 55% independents) as well as majorities of Becerra and Hilton supporters (65% to 69%) are following news about the gubernatorial candidates at least fairly closely.
House Races. When asked about US House races, likely voters say they would vote for the Democratic candidate over the Republican candidate by a 28 point margin (63% to 35%). Likely voter preferences were similar in September (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/) (62% Democrat, 36% Republican), July (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-the-environment-july-2026/) (63% Democrat, 35% Republican), May (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) (64% Democrat, 35% Republican), and February (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-february-2026/) (62% Democrat, 36% Republican). Today, nine in ten or more Democratic and Republican likely voters would choose their party’s House candidate, while most independent likely voters would vote for the Democratic candidate over the Republican candidate (58% to 37%). Majorities across demographic groups and major regions say they would vote for the Democratic candidate in their House district race, with the exception of those in the Inland Empire (47%).
With national attention focused on the 2026 midterms, 58 percent of California likely voters say they are more enthusiastic about voting than usual in the congressional elections (40% less enthusiastic). About half or more across demographic groups say they are more enthusiastic about voting than usual, but there is an “enthusiasm gap” across partisan groups (71% Democrats, 46% Republicans, 46% independents) and between those who would vote for the Democratic (69%) and the Republican (41%) House candidate. Sixty-one percent of likely voters were more enthusiastic about voting for Congress in May, (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) shortly before the June primary, and 52 percent were more enthusiastic in September 2024 (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-likely-voters-0924.pdf), ahead of the last congressional election. Today, about half or more across demographic groups and major state regions say they are more enthusiastic about voting than usual in the congressional elections.
Legislative Ballot Measures. We are also tracking support for five propositions that the state legislature placed on the November 3 ballot. Respondents read the full ballot titles and labels.
Proposition 1 (Authorizes Bonds for Housing Affordability Programs). Sixty percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative statute, which authorizes $11.25 billion in general obligation bonds for housing affordability programs; 38 percent would vote no. In the September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), 55 percent said they would vote yes and 43 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 1 varies across partisan groups (81% Democrats, 29% Republicans, 54% independents) and between homeowners and renters (54% to 77%). Majorities across demographic groups and the state’s major regions would vote yes on Proposition 1.
Proposition 2 (Increases Rainy Day Fund). Sixty-one percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative constitutional amendment, which increases the rainy day fund approved by voters in 2014; 38 percent would vote no. In the September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), 60 percent said they would vote yes and 39 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 2 varies across partisan groups (85% Democrats, 23% Republicans, 57% independents). Half or more would vote yes across the state’s major regions and age, gender, education, homeownership, income, and racial/ethnic groups.
Proposition 4 (Repeals Prohibition Against Public Funding of Election Campaigns) . Forty-five percent of likely voters would vote yes on this legislative statute, which repeals a prohibition on state and local governments offering public funding of candidate election campaigns; 52 percent would vote no. Borrow $8.4 billion for immunology research
Proposition 38 would create an $8.4 billion bond largely to fund research into fighting cancer, heart disease and Alzheimer’s, plus other diseases that can be treated through immunotherapies.

es across partisan groups (28% Democrats, 68% Republicans, 41% independents) and age groups (30% 18 to 34; 37% 35 to 54; 50% 55 and older) and is below 50 percent across regions.
When we asked likely voters which of the 14 state propositions they are most interested in, 14 percent chose one of the five legislative ballot measures (7% Proposition 1; 1% Proposition 2; 2% Proposition 4; 2% Proposition 5; 2% Proposition 43). Eighty-six percent are most interested in one of the nine citizens’ initiatives, with about half expressing the most interest in Proposition 39 (23%; Prohibits Citizens from Voting Unless They Present Government-Issued Identification) and Proposition 40 (22%; Imposes One-Time Tax). There are partisan divides in interest in Proposition 39 (13% Democrat, 47% Republican, 16% independents) and Proposition 40 (27% Democrats, 13% Republicans, 21% independents). Since the September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), the share of those most interested in Proposition 40 has increased (16% to 22%).
Citizens’ Initiatives on the November Ballot
In addition to the five legislative measures, voters are weighing in on nine citizens’ initiatives. Overwhelming majorities of California likely voters say that the voter information guide, which is mailed to voters by the California Secretary of State, is very (40%) or somewhat useful (48%; 12% not too useful). Most are very (26%) or somewhat satisfied (59%) with the information that is available to voters about citizens’ initiatives on the state ballot (14% not satisfied).
After reading the ballot title and label for Proposition 3 (Extending Tax on High Incomes), which would make temporary voter-approved tax rates for individuals earning over $371,000 permanent, a majority of likely voters in the state say they would vote yes; four in ten would vote no. Findings were similar in September 2026 (58% yes, 40% no). Today, most Democrats and independents support Proposition 3, while most Republicans oppose. Likely voters who earn less than $40,000 (77%), are age 18 to 34 (73%), or are renters (69%) are among the most likely to say they would vote yes. Majorities across regions are in support, though Central Valley residents are more divided (51% yes, 48% no).
Proposition 37 (Creates Loan Program for Middle-Income Home-Buyers), which would authorize $25 billion in bonds to offer eligible California residents fixed-rate mortgages for newly constructed homes below $1.5 million, is supported by about two in three likely voters (65% yes, 32% no). Support was similar in September (61% yes, 35% no). Majorities of Democrats (80%) and independents (54%) are in support; Republicans are more divided (47% yes, 51% no). Majorities across demographic and regional groups say they would vote yes on Proposition 37, and support declines with rising age and income.
A majority of likely voters (57%) would vote yes on Proposition 38 (Authorizes Bonds For Immunology Medical Research), which would authorize $8.4 billion in general obligation bonds. About four in ten would vote no (41%). The share in support is similar to a month ago (55% yes, September 2026). Today, partisans are divided (70% Democrats, 53% independents, 37% Republicans) and majorities across regions and demographic groups are in support of Proposition 38.
Fewer than half of likely voters in the state would vote yes (41%, 58% no) on Proposition 39 (Prohibits Citizens From Voting Unless They Present Government-Issued Identification) which would invalidate mail ballots that do not have the last four digits of a government-issued identification number written on the envelope and prohibits in-person voting without presenting government-issued identification. Shares were similar a month ago (43% yes, 55% no). Today, most Republicans would vote yes (82%), most Democrats would vote no (84%), and independents are divided (48% yes, 50% no). Majorities across most demographic groups would vote no, except for likely voters whose highest level of education is a high school diploma, who are more divided (48% yes, 49% no).
Proposition 40 (Imposes One-Time Tax), which would impose a 5 percent tax on certain taxpayers with assets over $1 billion, is supported by 46 percent of likely voters, while 52 percent would vote no. A slim majority was in support in September (52% yes, 46% no). Today, over six in ten Democrats would vote yes, compared to four in ten independents and about two in ten Republicans. Likely voters who are younger (70% 18 to 34), earn less than $40,000 (64%), are Latino (58%), or reside in Los Angeles (53%) are among the most likely to support this proposition.
Likely voters are divided on Proposition 41 (Prohibits New State Taxes Excluding Revenues from State Spending Limit), which would nullify state taxes enacted after January 1 this year that exempt their revenues from the voter-approved state spending limit and requires audits of programs funded by new special taxes (48% yes, 49% no). Support was similar in September (51% yes, 44% no). Today, most Republicans and independents support Proposition 41, compared to about three in ten Democrats. Support varies across demographic and regional groups.
A slim majority of likely voters would vote yes (51%, 47% no) on Proposition 42 (Prohibits New State Personal Property Taxes), which would prohibit new state taxes imposed on the ownership of personal property other than real estate. Support was similar a month ago (54% yes, 43% no). Today, most Republicans and independents would vote yes, while most Democrats would vote no. The share in support varies across demographic and regional groups.
Just a quarter of likely voters would vote yes (25%, 71% no) on Proposition 44 (Requires Community Health Clinics Spend 90% of Revenue on Program Services), which would impose penalties on nonprofit community clinics providing primary care to medically underserved areas and populations that spend less than 90 percent of revenue on program services. A majority was opposed in September (34% yes, 61% no). Today, six in ten or more across partisan, demographic, and regional groups would vote no.
Likely voters are divided (46% yes, 50% no) on Proposition 45 (Modifies Environmental Review), which would amend the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) to expedite environmental review for certain projects by setting deadlines to complete environmental review and resolve lawsuits challenging project approvals. Views were similar a month ago (49% yes, 46% no). A majority of Republicans would vote yes, while a majority of Democrats (54%) and half of independents (50%) would vote no. The shares in support vary across partisan, demographic, and regional groups.
State of the State
Ahead of the November election, about four in ten adults (45%) and likely voters (38%) choose cost of living, inflation, and the economy as the most important issue facing people in California today. Fewer choose housing costs and availability (12% adults, 13% likely voters). Cost of living is most likely to be chosen as the state’s top issue across parties, regions, and demographic groups.
When asked about the economic outlook for the next 12 months, most Californians are pessimistic, with three in four adults (77%) and likely voters (79%) expecting bad economic times. Seven in ten Californians have held this view since 2025. Today, two in three or more across parties, regions, and demographic groups are pessimistic.
Californians are also pessimistic about the outlook for the state, with about six in ten or fewer adults (59%) and likely voters (55%) saying the state is heading in the wrong direction. At least half of Californians have said the state is heading in the wrong direction since June 2023 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-june-2023/). About half or more across parties, regions, and demographic groups—except for Democrats (35%)—hold this pessimistic view.
Nearly all Californians view housing costs as a problem in their part of California, with a solid majority seeing them as a big problem (64%) and three in ten saying they are somewhat of a problem (32%). Just 4 percent say housing affordability is not a problem. Across regions, San Francisco Bay Area residents (71%) are the most likely to say housing costs are a big problem, while Central Valley residents (50%) are the least likely (Inland Empire: 68%, Los Angeles: 67%, Orange County/San Diego: 64%). The view that housing affordability is a big problem is widely held by about six in ten or more across parties and demographic groups.
With inflation on the rise again, most Californians continue to feel they are falling behind. Today, about three in four California adults (76%) and likely voters (73%) say their income is not keeping up with inflation, similar to results in February (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-february-2026/) (71% adults, 67% likely voters). This view is widely held, with seven in ten or more adults across regions and demographic groups saying their income has not kept up. This view is also shared across party lines (74% Democrats, 71% Republicans, 76% independents).
As Governor Newsom approaches the last months of his tenure—and as speculation about his political future swirls—just under half of adults and likely voters approve of his job performance (47% adults, 49% likely voters). Until now, majorities of Californians have approved of the governor since October 2025 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2025/). Today, about seven in ten Democrats, four in ten independents, and about one in ten Republicans approve of the governor. There are also regional differences: a majority of residents in the San Francisco Bay Area and Los Angeles approve, compared to fewer than half in the other regions.
Half or fewer adults and likely voters approve of the state legislature (42% adults, 46% likely voters) and the state legislators representing their assembly and senate districts (43% adults, 48% likely voters). About half of Californians have approved of the legislature since last October (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2025/), and views of state legislators were similar in May (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/). Today, about six in ten Democrats approve of the state legislature and their own legislators, compared to nearly four in ten independents and fewer than one in five Republicans.
When asked about their confidence in the system in which votes are cast and counted in California elections, six in ten likely voters have a great deal (42%) or quite a lot (21%) of confidence, while nearly four in ten have some confidence (15%) or very little confidence (22%). Seven in ten likely voters (71%)—with partisans divided—think it’s a good thing that a vote-by-mail ballot is mailed to every active registered voter before each election.
State of the Nation
Asked about the most important problem facing the US today, Californians are most likely to choose the economy, unemployment, and jobs (26%), followed by threats to democratic norms (18%) and corruption (14%). Across partisan groups, Democrats are most likely to choose threats to democratic norms (29%), while the economy is the top choice among independents (32%) and Republicans (25%). The economy is the top national issue across most regions and demographic groups.
A record-high share (82%) of California adults say the US is headed in the wrong direction (79% likely voters). Most Democrats (95%) and independents (85%) hold this view, whereas Republicans are divided (51% wrong direction, 48% right direction). Three in four or more across regions and demographic groups say the country is headed in the wrong direction. Californians (82%) are more likely to hold this pessimistic view than adults nationwide (72%), according to an October ABC News/Washington Post/Ipsos (https://www.ipsos.com/sites/default/files/ct/news/documents/2026-10/ABC-Post-Ipsos%20Trend%20Topline%2010.21.pdf) poll.
Only about three in ten adults say that people who share their political views in the US are extremely (9%) or very (22%) free to express them (likely voters: 11% extremely, 24% very). Conversely, similar shares believe that people who share their political views are a little (16% adults, 14% likely voters) or not at all free (13% adults, 11% likely voters) to openly express them. Three in ten adults and a third of likely voters (36%) believe people who share their views are somewhat free to express them. Views were similar among adults nationwide in a June Pew Research Center (https://www.pewresearch.org/journalism/2026/09/15/americans-value-press-freedom-but-differ-on-its-limits/) survey.
Most California adults say freedom of the press is at least somewhat important to the well-being of society (92% adults, 95% likely voters). While majorities across partisan groups share this view, Democrats (68%) are far more likely than independents (49%) and Republicans (27%) to say freedom of the press is extremely important.
When asked about the way democracy is working in the US, just three in ten adults (5% very, 26% somewhat) and likely voters (7% very, 25% somewhat) say they are satisfied. About seven in ten say they are not satisfied with democracy in the US (adults: 39% not too, 29% not at all; likely voters: 37% not too, 31% not at all). About three in four Democrats (79%) and independents (74%) express dissatisfaction, while a majority of Republicans (59%) are satisfied. Six in ten or more across regions and demographic groups are dissatisfied.
About two in ten California adults (21%) approve of the way Donald Trump is handling his job as president (26% likely voters)—a record low across both terms of his presidency. For comparison, Donald Trump’s approval rating stood at 29 percent in October 2018 (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-all-adults-1018.pdf). Today, overwhelming majorities of Democrats and independents disapprove of the president, while seven in ten Republicans approve.
Fewer approve of the way the US Congress is handling its job (16% adults, 17% likely voters). Two in ten or fewer have approved of Congress since June 2025 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-june-2025/). Today, majorities across partisan groups disapprove of the US Congress.
Three in ten adults (30%) and about four in ten likely voters (38%) approve of the way their own representative to the US House of Representatives is handling the job. Shares are similar among Californians who currently live in a Democratic-held seat and a Republican-held seat. Four in ten or fewer across regions and demographic groups approve of the way their own House representative is handling the job.
Three in four adults (75%) and seven in ten likely voters (72%) disapprove of US military action against Iran. Most Democrats (94%) and independents (74%) disapprove, while about two in three Republicans approve (65%). About two in three or more across regions and demographic groups disapprove. California adults are more likely than adults nationwide (61%) to disapprove, according to an October Reuters/Ipsos (https://www.ipsos.com/sites/default/files/ct/news/documents/2026-10/Reuters%20Ipsos%20News%20Issue%20Survey%20October%202026%20Topline_3.pdf) poll.
Three in four adults (75%) and seven in ten likely voters (71%) disapprove of the job that US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) is doing. Overall, seven in ten or more adults have disapproved since October 2025 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2025/). Today, most Democrats (95%) and independents (75%) disapprove, while most Republicans (72%) approve of ICE. Solid majorities across demographic and regional groups disapprove.
About two in three likely voters say they are very (25%) or somewhat (40%) confident that votes for Congress will be accurately counted nationwide. The share who are very confident has dropped from October 2024 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2024/) (38%).

Methodology

Proposition 38 would create an $8.4 billion bond largely to fund research into fighting cancer, heart disease and Alzheimer’s, plus other diseases that can be treated through immunotherapies. Half the money would go to a research institute affiliated with the University of California. The other half would be distributed to select public universities and nonprofits. Below are lists of the top 10 contributors to committees that have raised at least $1,000,000 and are primarily formed to support or oppose a state ballot measure or a candidate for state office in the November 2026 General Election.
The lists do not show all contributions to every state ballot measure, or each independent expenditure committee formed to support or oppose a state candidate, only those committees that have raised $1,000,000 or more and have at least one contributor of $10,000 or more.
For itemized contribution and expenditure reports on state ballot measures, go to the CA Secretary of State's Ballot Measure (https://cal-access.sos.ca.gov/Campaign/Measures/).
For itemized contribution and expenditure reports on state candidates, go to the CA Secretary of State's Candidate (https://cal-access.sos.ca.gov/Campaign/Candidates/).

Because of this, it is not possible to determine the amount of the contribution that was spent specifically on the campaign for any particular measure. content.thinking:
I'm noting a Berkeley IGS poll from August 17, 2026, showing 48% in favor and 41% opposed, taken from the Indivisible El Dorado page. That's an earlier reading than the others, so I want to check whether it predates the campaign's ramp-up.

I'm checking whether that August 17 Berkeley IGS poll, cited on the Indivisible El Dorado page, is a real Berkeley IGS release, since the IGS poll listings I've seen don't include it. I also want to see whether the October LA Times/Berkeley IGS poll asked about Prop 38 at all, because the tax questions I've seen skip it.

I'm checking the Emerson October 17–19 poll and the LA Times/Berkeley IGS poll for whether either asked about Prop 38, since the PPIC figure of 57-41 is the only result I have so far. I also want to see if the No on Prop 38 campaign's funding details, including the Robert Kaplan contribution, are reported consistently across sources.

I'm now looking at the Oct 5 contribution figures, the top Prop 38 support total of about $81.4 million, and the small No side funding of roughly $12K as of Oct 22. I also see the endorsement split: support from AAI, the state Democratic Party, City of Hope and the Michelson Center, against the League of Women Voters and several major newspapers, which would be a notably one-sided editorial front.

I'm weighing the "No" side's position: it has much of the editorial establishment and good-government groups behind it but very little money, while the "Yes" side has a large funding edge, bipartisan party endorsements, and patient-advocacy backing. I'm also thinking about whether the CalMatters pieces on bond volume and a single-nonprofit allocation might shed light on voter fatigue or the context around this measure.

Proposition 38 authorizes California to issue an $8.4 billion general obligation bond to fund medical research in immunology and immunotherapy, with state payments taken from the state General Fund. The measure mandates that at least $4.2 billion be dedicated specifically to research on cancer, heart disease, and Alzheimer’s disease, while capping state administrative expenditures at 2 percent. The bond proceeds are divided equally between a designated specialized research institute selected by the California Department of Public Health (https://www.cdph.ca.gov/) that meets specific size, funding, and University of California (https://www.universityofcalifornia.edu/) (UC) collaboration criteria, while the remaining half is distributed as competitive research grants to California universities and non-profit research institutions via an advisory council.
Proposition 38 mandates that the institute generate as much revenue as possible from the funded research. Ten percent of this revenue would go to the state’s General Fund until the research bond is repaid. Additional funding would be used for future immunotherapy and immunology research. Grant recipients are required to purchase at least half of their goods and services from California suppliers whenever feasible, and any treatments developed through this research and sold within California must generally be offered to patients at a 20 percent discount. Both the designated institute and the grant council are subject to annual public reporting and independent financial audit requirements. Both the designated institute and the grant council are subject to annual public reporting and independent financial audit requirements.
F iscal Impact
(Summary of Legislative Analyst's Estimate of Net State and Local Government Fiscal Impact)
If Proposition 38 passes, the state General Fund would incur an estimated annual repayment cost of $500 million to $600 million over roughly 20 years to pay off the bond. This would amount to about 0.25% of the state's total General Fund budget and approximately 10% more total cost (adjusted for inflation) than upfront funding due to interest. Offsetting these expenditures, the state could potentially earn significant revenue from commercialized research treatments funded by the measure, though the amount and timing remain uncertain and could take decades to materialize. Additionally, the initiative would generate indirect fiscal effects on state health programs like Medi-Cal, where net costs could rise or fall depending on the pricing and adoption of newly developed medical treatments.
What your vote means
YES: A YES vote supports issuing $8.4 billion in state general obligation bonds for immunology and immunotherapy research, allocating half of the funds to a University of California-affiliated research institute and distributing the remainder as grants to California public and nonprofit medical research institutions.
NO: A NO vote opposes issuing $8.4 billion in state bonds to fund immunology and immunotherapy research and treatment development.

I'm checking the Desert Sun article from October 28, 2026, which has a PPIC table of findings on other ballot measures, not the Berkeley IGS poll. The IGS release from October 29 covered seven propositions, so I need to work out which seven they were, starting with the numbers from the Mercury News piece.

I'm working through which seven propositions the IGS poll measured. So far I have Props 3, 39, 40, 41, 42 and 43 from the numbers, with Prop 45 ruled out, and I still need to identify the seventh.

I'm now weighing whether Prop 38 was among the IGS measures, since a result under 50% for it would matter for the Yes side. The Mercury News snippet about the billionaires tax doesn't mention it, so I'll fetch the Mercury News and Desert Sun articles and the IGS release to check.

I'm also considering whether an LA Times report from October 29 might settle whether Prop 38 was measured and what it got, since the Mercury News snippet doesn't mention it.

content.text: The release lists seven measured propositions but the snippets don't name them all. I'll check the Mercury News and LA Times coverage of the Oct 29 poll and search for Prop 38's number in it.

California’s proposed billionaires tax is losing support days before Election Day, according to the second major independent poll released this week.
Thursday’s poll by the Institute of Governmental Studies at UC Berkeley found 42% of likely voters in favor of Proposition 40 and 50% opposed (https://escholarship.org/uc/item/72722408), with 8% undecided. In a mid-September Berkeley IGS poll, 45% of likely voters favored Proposition 40, while 42% were opposed and 13% were undecided. It would need majority support to pass.
The measure would impose a one-time, 5% tax on the wealth of California billionaires.
A pair of statewide measures aimed at blocking Proposition 40, Proposition 41 and Proposition 42, remained short of the needed majority support, with opposition mounting, the poll found.
Proposition 41 had support from 38% of likely voters while 47% were opposed and 16% were undecided, compared to IGS’ mid-September poll in which 37% were in favor, 33% opposed and 30% undecided. Proposition 42 support remained at 43% as it was in September, while opposition rose to 45% from 34% and undecided fell to 12% from 23% last month.
Both also require majorities to pass. If either passes and receives more “yes” votes than Proposition 40, it could prevent the wealth tax from taking effect if courts find the measures conflict.

Amid wealthy opponents’ ad blitz, Prop. 40 is losing ground (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/27/california-billionaires-tax-prop-40-poll/)
“These results suggest that neither the advocates of the wealth tax nor those seeking to block future taxes have managed to persuade a majority of voters to their sides,” IGS Co-Director Eric Schickler said. “This may reflect an electorate unhappy with the wealth and power of billionaires but also not sold on a specific solution.”
The poll was conducted online in English and Spanish Oct. 19-25, 2026, among 2,787 registered voters, of whom a weighted subset of 1,477 had either already voted or were considered likely to vote in the state’s Nov. 3 election. The margin of error was plus or minus 3 percentage points for the subset of surveyed likely voters.
It is the second poll this week to find support for the Proposition 40 billionaires tax fading. A Public Policy Institute of California poll Tuesday found that support for Proposition 40 had fallen to 46% from 52% in a September PPIC poll (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/27/california-billionaires-tax-prop-40-poll/), while opposition had risen to 52% from 46% last month. That poll also found support slipping and opposition mounting to Propositions 41 and 42, though it found Proposition 42 maintaining narrow majority support among likely voters.
Nearly $400 million has been spent collectively on the three measures, among the most closely watched contests on the state ballot.
Proposition 40 is sponsored by SEIU United Healthcare Workers West (https://yeson40.com/?gad_source=1&gad_campaignid=24260871789&gbraid=0AAAABC2lkj1e3wEbPnCvZ-bOGGsaK_t-C&gclid=Cj0KCQjw3YvXBhCDARIsAKB-ox9nBHZ3OyEIQScw49n6D-MdfgBQwJMBaAh2pUa8NPlFM70x2-SIRhkaAj4cEALw_wcB), which says it would help offset federal Medicaid cuts. It would impose a one-time, 5% tax, payable over five years with interest, on an estimated more than 200 Californians and certain trusts with a net worth — the total value of all assets and property interests worldwide — of $1 billion or more who lived in the state as of Jan. 1, 2026. Supporters include the California Nurses Association, independent Vermont U.S. Sen. Bernie Sanders and Rep. Ro Khanna, a Fremont Democrat.
Opponents (https://votenoon40.org/?&utm_medium=paid-search&utm_content=A18&utm_campaign=NoOn40&gad_source=1&gad_campaignid=24164855903&gbraid=0AAAABEizAVbUeWDtCbY6DbtURFUEQVEPx&gclid=Cj0KCQjw3YvXBhCDARIsAKB-ox_dANRzR4IFRvRvjuHz_CZLLCxIH87pCX5Z85gPQ8lzTiWKkED9jxEaAp18EALw_wcB) include Gov. Gavin Newsom, the California Teachers Association and both candidates for governor — Democratic former Health Secretary Xavier Becerra and Republican former Fox News host Steve Hilton. They’ve said such a one-time, California-only tax wouldn’t provide recurring new funding and would drive wealthy innovators and job creators, hefty contributors to the state’s income tax revenues, to other states.
Proposition 41 would prohibit new state taxes that exempt their revenues from California’s spending limit and require audits of programs funded by new special taxes. Proposition 42 would prohibit new state taxes on the ownership of personal property, such as financial assets, and limit certain retroactive taxes.
While likely voters were cooling on the billionaires tax, support remained steady for Proposition 3, which would make permanent higher income tax rates on high earners that voters initially approved in 2012, then extended in 2016 until 2030. The higher rates kick in at incomes of $371,000 for single filers and $743,000 for joint filers, increasing the rate on income above those thresholds from 9.3% to 10.3%. The top rates, which increased to 12.3% from 9.3%, kick in at $743,000 for single filers and $1.5 million for joint filers.
The IGS poll found that support for Proposition 3 has held steady at 54% while opposition has edged up slightly to 37% from 34%, and 8% remain undecided.
Support for another statewide measure aimed at limiting local tax measures, Proposition 43, continues to trail opposition, the poll found. Proposition 43 would require two-thirds approval for local special taxes proposed through citizen initiatives, which currently can pass by a simple majority. Special taxes, which fund specific purposes, already require two-thirds approval when proposed by local governing bodies.
The IGS poll found that while support for Proposition 43 grew to 36%, opposition also grew to 46%. In September, 31% were in favor and 40% opposed.
While the poll focused on tax-related measures, it also asked about another closely watched initiative, Proposition 39, which would require voter identification. Support slipped to 37% while opposition grew to 57% with just 5% undecided. In September, 39% were in favor, 52% opposed and 9% undecided.
Proposition 4, which would repeal a state prohibition against public financing for election campaigns, had 41% support and 35% opposition in the latest poll.
