California ballot measures election night results, live updates
Voting is underway in California, where voters will decide on a slate of ballot measures.
Polls close at 8 p.m. Tuesday. However, it may remain unclear whether Tuesday night will bring California's ballot-measure results. California's vote-counting process (https://www.desertsun.com/story/news/nation/california/2026/06/03/why-california-takes-so-long-to-finalize-primary-election-results/90388044007/) often continues for weeks after Election Day as election officials process and tally millions of ballots.
As voters weigh 14 statewide ballot measures, two proposals have drawn particular attention: one that would impose a one-time tax on California billionaires and another that would require voters to present additional identification to cast a ballot.
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Here's what to know about California's statewide ballot measures.
Proposition 40: the 'billionaire tax' measure
Proposition 40 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop40-text-proposed-laws.pdf) would impose a one-time 5% tax on residents whose net worth exceeds $1 billion. The tax would apply to people who were California residents as of Jan. 1, 2026.
Real estate, pensions, and retirement accounts would generally be exempt, according to the Legislative Analyst's Office. Taxpayers could opt to pay the tax, due in 2027, over five years, but would have to pay more.
Ninety percent of the revenue would go to health care programs, while the remaining 10% would go to education and food assistance programs.
Two countermeasures to the proposed wealth tax, Propositions 41 and 42, have also qualified for the November ballot. The initiatives are intended to limit the effects of Proposition 40 if voters approve it. Proposition 41 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/41/) would prohibit new state taxes that exclude revenue from the state spending limit, while Proposition 42 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/42/) would prohibit new personal property taxes and certain retroactive state taxes passed after January 2026.
Advertisement
Advertisement
Early polling shows voters are split on the measure. A Citrin-POLITICO poll (https://www.politico.com/newsletters/california-playbook/2026/10/19/the-billionaire-tax-isnt-breaking-through-01125880) released Monday, Oct. 19, found that 46% of likely voters favor the measure, while 43% oppose it. A separate Independent VoterProject survey (https://www.desertsun.com/story/news/politics/elections/2026/10/05/becerra-leads-hilton-but-governor-race-may-be-tightening-poll-finds/92102112007/) released Oct. 5 also found voters split over the measure, with 40% in favor and 38% opposed.
However, recent polling suggests support for Proposition 40 has weakened in the campaign's final weeks.
According to a Public Policy Institute of California Poll (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2026/) released Oct. 28, Proposition 40 is opposed by 52% of likely voters and supported by 46%. A poll from the UC Berkeley Institute of Governmental (https://escholarship.org/uc/item/1vp9q3f9) Studies, released the following day, found a similar result: 50% of likely voters intend to vote against the measure, while 42% are in favor.
Proposition 39: the Voter ID initiative
California is one of 14 states (https://ballotpedia.org/Voter_identification_laws_by_state) that do not require voters to present identification to cast a ballot.
Advertisement
Advertisement
According to the state's voter information guide, if passed by voters, Proposition 39 would (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop39.pdf):
Require voters casting a mail-in ballot to provide a government-issued ID number.
Invalidate mail ballots should the ID number on the ballot envelope not match the ID number used when registering.
Require voters casting a ballot in person to show a government-issued ID.
Require election officials to report each year how many voters' citizenship statuses have been verified in each county.
Recent polling on Proposition 39 has shown the measure failing.
A UC Berkeley IGS poll (https://escholarship.org/uc/item/1vp9q3f9) released Oct. 29 found the Voter ID initiative trailing by a wide 20-percentage-point margin, with 57% of voters opposed and 37% in favor. A Public Policy Institute of California Poll (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2026/) released a day earlier shows Proposition 39 with fewer than half of likely voters in support: 41% in favor and 58% opposed. The poll's findings are similar to those from the PPIC poll released a month earlier, which found 43% of voters in support of the initiative and 55% opposed.
Wealth tax, voter ID election night results
On Election Night, check back here to see how the statewide initiatives are faring. First results are expected to come in shortly after 8 p.m. with continued updates through Tuesday night.
Proposition 40 (and its two countermeasures)
Proposition 40 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/40/index.htm) would impose a one-time 5% tax on California billionaires' wealth. The funds would largely go toward health care.
Advertisement
Advertisement
Proposition 41 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/41/index.htm) would nullify certain state taxes enacted after Jan. 1, 2026, if their revenues are exempt from California's voter-approved spending cap. It would also require audits before and after implementing new special tax-funded programs.
Proposition 42 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/42/index.htm) would prohibit new state taxes on personal property and ban retroactive state taxes based on past actions. If passed, it would also invalidate taxes enacted after Jan. 1, 2026, that conflict with these rules.
Proposition 39
Proposition 39 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/39/index.htm) would require voters to present additional identification to cast a ballot. If passed, the measure would require in-person voters to present government-issued ID and would invalidate mail-in ballots without the last four digits of a designated government-issued ID written on the envelope.
California voters weigh in on 10 other measures
Here's how the 10 other propositions on the ballot are playing out on election night.
Proposition 1
If passed, Proposition 1 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/1/index.htm) would let the state borrow $11.25 billion to fund housing affordability programs, including multifamily rental housing, mortgages for veterans, supportive housing, preserving existing affordable housing, and down payment assistance.
Proposition 2
Proposition 2 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/2/index.htm) proposes doubling California's Rainy Day Fund, first approved by voters in 2014. The funds would support education, health care, public safety, and other essential services during economic downturns.
Proposition 3
Proposition 3 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/3/index.htm) would make the tax rates voters approved in 2012 for residents earning more than $371,000 annually permanent, rather than letting them expire in 2031.
Proposition 4
Proposition 4 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/4/index.htm) would repeal the ban on state and local governments using public money to help fund election campaigns. However, public funding for the campaigns could not come from money set aside for education, transportation, or public safety.
Proposition 5
Current law allows voters to elect replacement candidates at the same time as a recall election. Proposition 5 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/5/index.htm) would let voters fill recall vacancies through a special election or appointment.
Proposition 37
Proposition 37 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/37/index.htm) would create a new homebuying assistance program and authorize $25 billion in bonds to help eligible Californians buy newly built homes with fixed-rate mortgages covering up to 17% of the purchase price. The bonds would be repaid through mortgage payments, not state tax dollars.
Proposition 38
Proposition 38 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/38/index.htm) would allow the state to borrow $8.4 billion for immunology and immunotherapy research. Half of the funds would go to a single University of California-affiliated nonprofit medical research institute and the other half to research grants.
Proposition 43
Proposition 43 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/43/index.htm) would raise the vote threshold for citizen-driven local special-tax initiatives from a simple majority to a two-thirds supermajority starting Jan. 1, 2027.
Proposition 44
Proposition 44 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/44/index.htm) would require Federally Qualified Health Centers (community clinics that provide primary care to medically underserved areas and populations) to spend at least 90% of their annual revenue on health care services.
Proposition 45
Proposition 45 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/45/index.htm) would amend the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) to speed up environmental review for certain housing, transportation, water, and health projects by setting deadlines for reviews and for resolving lawsuits that challenge project approvals.
When do polls close?
Polls close (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/voting-resources/voting-california/help-strengthen-our-democracy/poll-worker-training-standards/section-three) at 8 p.m. on Tuesday, Nov. 3.
When will California election results be certified?
Thursday, Dec. 3, is the last day for county election officials to certify election results (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/upcoming-elections/general-election-november-3-2026/key-dates-deadlines), which must be sent to the California Secretary of State by Dec. 4. The official certified results of the election will be posted by Friday, Dec. 11, at sos.ca.gov/elections. (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections)

Is Prop. 38 unconstitutional? Opponents take immunology bond fight to AG
By Tarini Mehta
Updated October 8, 2026 11:13 AM
California Attorney General Rob Bonta on Tuesday, Feb. 10, 2026, in Sacramento.
JOSÉ LUIS VILLEGAS
jvillegas@sacbee.com
The Yes on Proposition 38 campaign has raised more than $38 million and spent nearly $20 million of it on television advertisements (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=t-9WZJcETxc) in support of the $8.4 billion immunology research bond (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/election/voter-guide/article317117396.html) on the November ballot.
The No on Proposition 38 group had raised less than $640 by Sept. 19. Instead of funding ads, the group is focused on letter-writing campaigns to highlight possible issues with the ballot initiative.
On Oct. 6, they wrote a letter to California Attorney General Rob Bonta alleging that the measure may violate the state constitution.
“The stakes are substantial,” committee co-chair David Panush wrote. “Californians are being asked to assume $8.4 billion in general obligation bond debt, with half the proceeds reserved for what appears to be a single, predetermined private institution. Voters deserve to know whether this arrangement complies with the constitutional safeguards governing initiatives and the use of public funds.”
Supporters of the proposition, meanwhile, said the letter was a “campaign stunt to distract voters.”
The proposition will ask voters to allow the state to borrow $8.4 billion to support medical research in immunology and immunotherapy conducted by California research institutes and universities.
Its backers say the measure materialized as a response to the Trump administration’s cuts and freezes to thousands of research grants — many of which were later restored, but not without creating disruptions and delays. The stated goal is to allow immunology research to cure and prevent diseases like cancer and Alzheimer’s to advance unimpeded. Half of the bond proceeds would go to a single nonprofit immunology research institute affiliated with the University of California, while the rest would be distributed as competitive research grants to public or nonprofit universities and institutions.
Earlier this summer, CalMatters reported only one research institute in California (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/07/proposition-38-california/) appeared to meet the criteria for half of the immunology bond’s funds: the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy, an independent medical research organization affiliated with UCLA. Gary Michelson, a billionaire philanthropist and medical inventor, is both the co-founder of that institute and the chief backer of Prop. 38.
Last month, the opponents sent a letter to the UC Board of Regents urging them to only approve additional funding or construction commitments for the CIII if it agrees to public transparency and conflict-of-interest safeguards that public agencies are subject to. The UC board approved next steps in the construction of the institute’s facility at its September meeting.
Violation of constitution?
In a letter this week, Panush urged Bonta to weigh in on if Prop. 38 violates the California Constitution before voters decide to approve it. The attorney general is involved in the ballot initiative process in California from the very beginning. For any initiative proposed by citizens to make it onto the ballot, it must first be submitted to the attorney general with a request to prepare a title and summary that can be circulated to collect signatures — a step that was taken months ago for the immunology bond.
Suggesting Bonta take another look at the measure, Panush cited a section of the California Constitution that says an initiative that identifies a private corporation to perform any function or have any power may not be submitted to voters. While Prop. 38 does not name any private corporation, he asked if it “makes any legal difference when the requirements effectively identify it.”
For the institute that will receive half the bond proceeds if Prop. 38 passes, the measure outlined several specific requirements. The nonprofit immunology research institute must be affiliated with a University of California campus that has a hospital and clinic volume of more than 35,000 inpatient admissions and 3,500,000 outpatient visits each year. It must also own or lease a site that is at least 200,000 square feet in size and note philanthropic funding of at least $250 million in its affiliation agreement with the UC. And it must have secured $50 million to support a rapid vaccine development program and another $50 million for a microbiome research program.
“That would mean an institute connected to a health system with, say, 3 million visits, or occupying 180,000 square feet, would be excluded regardless of its research capabilities,” Panush said. “These thresholds operate as categorical exclusions, not measures of an institute’s scientific merit.”
In a previous interview with The Sacramento Bee (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article317199654.html), a spokesperson for the Yes on Proposition 38 campaign said the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy very likely meets the criteria, but the ultimate decision will be taken by the California Department of Public Health. If the state is unable to identify a suitable institute, it can modify the criteria, per the measure.
In its affiliation agreement with the UC, the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy is described as a “nonprofit public benefit corporation” governed independently of the university. First announced in 2024, the CIII is currently under construction and scheduled to open “in a year or so,” according to Yes on Proposition 38 spokesperson Robin Swanson. The institute is operational and has already administered grants, she said. A UC report indicates that construction will be complete by the end of 2028.
The UC, which sponsored a law to place a $7.5 billion scientific research bond (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article317049270.html) on the March 2028 ballot, said it does not have position on Prop. 38.
‘Saved my life’
For the supporters of the measure, the central campaign message has been that it will provide critical funding for time-sensitive immunology research. This includes finding cures for cancer, heart disease and Alzheimer’s disease.
“Prop 38 will provide much-needed funding to accelerate medical research at California’s world-class universities and research institutes, which is desperately needed in the face of federal research cuts,” Swanson said.
In a moving advertisement, cancer survivor Andrew Dale says immunotherapy saved his life and allowed him to see his daughter graduate from high school. Laurie Adami, a cancer survivor who spoke with The Bee last month, said Prop. 38 will benefit not just California (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article317199654.html), but the country and the whole world.
The measure is supported by a broad coalition of doctors, nurses and patient advocates. This includes the Alzheimer’s Association, ALS Association, the Michael J. Fox Foundation for Parkinson’s Research, American Nurses Association California, Prostate Cancer Foundation and Kidney Cancer Association. It also has the endorsement of the California Republican Party and the California Democratic Party. The Yes on Proposition 38 campaign contributed $250,000 to the Democratic Party in September.
The campaign had raised more than $38 million, as of Sept. 19, of which more than $33 million has come from billionaire philanthropist Gary Michelson and his nonprofit Michelson Center for Public Policy. Another $5 million was donated by Meyer Luskin, co-founder of the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy.
The campaign has spent nearly $20 million on cable airtime and advertisement production costs. It also spent more than $10 million earlier this year to circulate its petition and collect enough signatures to get onto the ballot.

I'm checking the Prop 14 result, which passed 51.1–48.9 in 2020, and I want the PPIC October 2020 poll figure for it. The PPIC survey I'm recalling covered Prop 15 (49% yes, 45% no), so I'm not sure it included Prop 14, and I'm looking for that number specifically.

I'm noting that the Berkeley IGS summary says no polls were available for Prop 14, so I'll check whether PPIC's October 2020 survey covered it. The No side has raised very little money, under $640 by September and about $12,000 by late October, and is relying mostly on letter-writing. Several groups and newspapers oppose it, while the Yes side has spent heavily on TV.

Prop 14 (2020) had plenty of Yes-side money and little organized opposition, yet it only squeaked by at 51%, unlike Prop 71's 59%. That suggests medical research bonds don't reliably draw overwhelming support, though the 2020 presidential-year electorate differed from a 2026 midterm, which may lean Democratic given the enthusiasm gap and Trump's low approval.

Now I'm working out the partisan breakdown: Democrats at about 70% yes, independents near 53%, Republicans around 37%, which weights to roughly 58% overall, close to the 57% topline. Next I'm thinking about how the final two weeks might shift things, with the Yes side still spending heavily on TV while the No side has almost no money and the editorial boards and HJTA are against it.

I'm weighing whether HJTA's opposition could move voters, though bond opposition from them rarely sways a majority, and their spending looks minimal at under $12,000. I'm also considering whether the billionaire framing around Michelson might make voters skeptical, while the Yes side's cancer-survivor ads probably keep them ahead. Next I want to check whether PPIC's likely-voter poll is a reliable benchmark for this.

Next I'm pulling the PPIC historical polls to see how their October numbers usually compared with final results on bonds and initiatives from 2014 to 2024, starting with the 2024 school bond.

Now I'm listing PPIC October figures against final results for several recent propositions, including the 2024 school bond, the climate bond, and the local bond threshold measure, to see how the poll numbers tended to shift.

Now I'm going through PPIC's October numbers against the final results for past propositions, with the 2020 stem cell bond still unknown, and I'm checking whether the 2020 measures on affirmative action, property tax, and gig workers moved between October and election day.

I'm now going through PPIC's October figures against final results for older propositions, checking 2018 measures like the gas tax repeal, rent control, and the dialysis initiative to see how the poll numbers tended to shift.

Now I'm going back over PPIC's October numbers for older propositions, comparing them with final results, with the 2016 and 2014 bond and tax measures next in line.

I'm estimating the chance that the measure still wins: a final result under 50% would take a drop of about seven points from the October poll, which I'd put at maybe 15–25%. The stable 55–57% support and the Yes side's large funding edge make me think it likely holds, so I'd put passage somewhere around 70–80%. The Prop 14 (2020) analog is the wrinkle I still need to settle.

Now I'm planning to check the PPIC October 2020 poll for how Prop 14 was polling before the election, to see whether a drop toward the final 51% result happened. I'll look at the PDF to find the Prop 14 figure.

PPIC STATEWIDE SURVEY: CALIFORNIANS AND THEIR GOVERNMENT
Voters Remain Divided on “Split Roll” Property Tax; Reinstating
Affirmative Action Still Trails
BIDEN HOLDS WIDE LEAD, WITH ENTHUSIASM HIGH ABOUT VOTING IN PRESIDENTIAL ELECTION
SAN FRANCISCO, October 21, 2020—With Election Day less than two weeks away, Californians remain
divided on a ballot measure that would change how commercial property is taxed. On another closely
watched ballot measure, reinstating affirmative action in the public sector has gained slightly since
September, but still has less than majority support. These are among the key findings of a statewide
survey released today by the Public Policy Institute of California.
Proposition 15 would change the tax assessment of commercial and industrial property by basing it on
current market value instead of purchase price—creating a “split roll” tax. Among likely voters, 49
percent are in favor, 45 percent oppose, and 6 percent are undecided. The margin was somewhat wider
in September (51% yes, 40% no, 9% undecided). Democrats (71%) are far more likely to say they would
vote yes than independents (42%) or Republicans (18%). Less than half of homeowners (41%) approve,
compared with 64 percent of renters. Younger Californians are more likely than older residents to
approve (60% ages 18 to 44, 42% 45 and older). Across regions, 55 percent of likely voters in Los
Angeles would vote yes, as would about half in Orange/San Diego (53%), the San Francisco Bay Area
(50%), and the Inland Empire (48%); 42 percent of likely voters in the Central Valley would vote yes.
“Californians remain closely divided on Proposition 15 as its proponents and opponents make their
closing arguments to voters over the next few weeks,” said Mark Baldassare, PPIC president and CEO.
Proposition 16 would repeal Proposition 209, a 1996 constitutional amendment that banned the use of
affirmative action involving race-based or sex-based preferences in the public sector. Among likely
voters, 37 percent would vote yes and 50 percent would vote no, with 12 percent undecided. This is a
slight gain from September, when 31 percent said yes, 47 percent said no, and 22 percent were
undecided. Today, 61 percent of Democratic likely voters support Proposition 16 (up from 46% in
September), compared with 22 percent of independents and 11 percent of Republicans (both similar to
September). Support is highest among likely voters in Los Angeles (41%) and the San Francisco Bay
Area (40%), followed by the Inland Empire (35%), Central Valley (33%), and Orange/San Diego (32%).
“Proposition 16 support has grown slightly but still falls short of a majority, with Democrats more in
favor and most Republicans and independents opposed to the measure,” Baldassare said.
Views on Confirming Barrett for Supreme Court Break along Partisan
Lines, while Majorities across Parties Oppose Overturning Roe v. Wade
Last month, President Trump nominated Judge Amy Coney Barrett to the US Supreme Court. About
four in ten Californians (41% adults, 41% likely voters) believe the Senate should confirm Barrett, while
PPIC STATEWIDE SURVEY OCTOBER 2020
PPIC.ORG/SURVEY Californians and Their Government 4
47 percent of adults and 54 percent of likely voters believe the Senate should not confirm. Views vary
widely by party affiliation, with 84 percent of Republicans, 44 percent of independents, and 16 percent
of Democrats saying the Senate should confirm.
Judge Barrett’s nomination has resurfaced the issue of whether Roe v. Wade, the landmark 1973
abortion rights ruling, could be overturned. An overwhelming majority of Californians (70%) say Roe v.
Wade should not be overturned. Across partisan groups, overwhelming majorities of Democrats (89%)
and independents (77%) and a slim majority of Republicans (53%) do not want the ruling overturned.
“Partisans are divided on the Supreme Court nominee, while majorities across party lines say that the
Supreme Court should not overturn Roe v. Wade,” Baldassare said.
Next month, the Supreme Court will hear a case challenging the constitutionality of the Affordable Care Act
(ACA), the 2010 federal health reform law. A solid majority of Californians (60%) have a favorable view of the
ACA, while a third (34%) have an unfavorable view. Across partisan groups, 88 percent of Democrats, 55
percent of independents, and 19 percent of Republicans have a favorable view.
Two in Three Are Concerned about COVID-19 Vaccine Being Rushed
A number of efforts to develop a COVID-19 vaccine are underway, with one or more vaccines possibly
available by the end of the year. Governor Newsom has announced the launch of an expert scientific
panel to independently review federally approved vaccines. Most Californians say they would definitely
(26%) or probably (31%) get the vaccine if it were available today, while a smaller share would probably
not (20%) or definitely not (20%) get the vaccine. Nationwide, a slim majority of adults say they would
definitely (21%) or probably (30%) get a vaccine if available, according to a Pew Research Center poll in
September.
At least half of Californians across party lines say they would either definitely or probably get a COVID-
19 vaccine if one were available today: 56 percent of both Democrats and independents and 50 percent
of Republicans. Across racial/ethnic groups, there are sharp differences: 70 percent of Asian Americans,
62 percent of whites, and 54 percent of Latinos say they would definitely or probably get a vaccine if
available today, with 29 percent of African Americans saying definitely or probably.
Asked about vaccine development, two-thirds of Californians (68%) are more concerned about
approval of a vaccine moving too fast, without fully ensuring safety and effectiveness, while one in four
(26%) are more concerned about approval moving too slowly, delaying access to a vaccine. Views vary
across party lines, but majorities are in agreement: 82 percent of Democrats, 73 percent of
independents, and 51 percent of Republicans are more concerned about approval moving too fast.
“One-quarter say they will definitely get the COVID-19 vaccine, with reluctance crossing party lines,
and two in three fear that approval will move too fast,” Baldassare said.
Biden Maintains Wide Lead over Trump, with Record-High Share of
Californians More Enthusiastic about Voting than Usual
As the candidates prepare for the final presidential debate tomorrow, Joe Biden maintains a sizeable
lead over Donald Trump, with 58 percent of likely voters favoring Biden/Harris and 32 percent favoring
Trump/Pence—very similar to September (60% Biden/Harris; 31% Trump/Pence). Biden leads by wide
margins in the San Francisco Bay Area (71% to 21%) and Los Angeles (70% to 22%), with narrower leads
in Orange/San Diego (50% to 37%) and the Inland Empire (48% to 42%). Trump has a narrow lead in the
Central Valley (44% to 38%).
Asked whether they are more enthusiastic or less enthusiastic than usual about voting in this
November’s presidential election, 72 percent of likely voters say they are more enthusiastic—a record
high in PPIC surveys. By comparison, four years ago in October 2016, 49 percent were more
PPIC STATEWIDE SURVEY OCTOBER 2020
PPIC.ORG/SURVEY Californians and Their Government 5
enthusiastic than usual. Majorities across party lines say they are more enthusiastic than usual this year:
79 percent of Democrats, 74 percent of Republicans, and 59 percent of independents.
“About three out of four say that they are more enthusiastic about voting in this presidential election,
with sharp increases across party lines compared to four years ago,” Baldassare said.
If the election for the US House of Representatives were held today, most likely voters (58%) would
vote for or lean toward the Democratic candidate; more than a third (37%) would vote for or lean
toward the Republican candidate. This is similar to September (60% Democratic, 33% Republican). In
the eight California House districts considered competitive according to the Cook Political Report
(districts 4, 10, 21, 22, 25, 39, 48, and 50), likely voters are divided: 49 percent favor the Republican, and
47 percent favor the Democrat. This is similar to September (54% Republican, 42% Democrat).
Californians See COVID-19 and Jobs and the Economy as Top Issues
Facing the State; Outlook for the State Is Brighter than for the US
When asked to identify the most important issue facing the state, COVID-19 (20%) and jobs and the
economy (16%) were named by more Californians than other issues. Following these are
environment/pollution/global warming (7%), homelessness (6%), housing costs/availability (6%), state
budget/deficit/spending (6%), and wildfires/fires (5%).
Amid the pandemic and a damaging wildfire season, Californians are somewhat split on whether the
state is going in the right direction or the wrong direction: 55 percent of adults and 50 percent of likely
voters say right direction, while 39 percent of adults and 46 percent of likely voters say wrong direction.
Democrats (73%) are far more likely than independents (47%) and Republicans (13%) to say right
direction. Across racial/ethnic groups, solid majorities of Asian Americans (68%), African Americans
(65%), and Latinos (60%) say right direction, while whites are divided (48% right direction, 48% wrong
direction).
In contrast to generally divided views on the state outlook, solid majorities (62% adults, 72% likely
voters) of Californians think the nation is heading in the wrong direction; 33 percent of adults and 25
percent of likely voters say the nation is heading in the right direction.

I've ruled out the PPIC October 2020 poll as a comparison, since its press release covered Props 15 and 16 but not Prop 14. Now I'm looking at whether PPIC has published a general analysis of how its final polls compared with results for initiatives.

I'm now recalling research on how ballot measure support tends to shift over a campaign, with "yes" shares often dropping by Election Day. I'd like to check that finding and how large the typical decline is, since this October poll's 16-point lead would need to flip to lose.

I'm estimating the chance the measure fails from its 16-point October lead, taking a 16-point swing as roughly a 5 to 15 percent risk and putting passage around 85 to 95 percent. That seems high, so I'm weighing the late-campaign shifts and how much uncertainty the final poll really carries before I settle on a number.

I'm checking whether any past California propositions that had a double-digit lead in PPIC's last poll ended up failing, and the examples I'm recalling aren't clear enough yet to count.

I'm now comparing Prop 15's slide from +11 in September to +4 in October and then its failure, which suggests a 16-point lead can erode fast when the opposition is well funded. I'm also weighing whether Prop 38's weaker opposition money makes that kind of collapse less likely here.

I'm going through a few more past California propositions with late PPIC polls, checking whether the ones that trailed or narrowly led in October ended up losing. Prop 56 and Prop 47 both sat near the outcomes I'd expect, while Prop 61 and the rent-control and gas-tax measures fell short with weaker October numbers.

I'm sizing up a few more past California propositions against their final PPIC numbers, and the record looks mixed rather than clean. For measures with a double-digit lead in the last poll, I'm estimating the failure rate at roughly 10 to 15 percent. I also want to check Prop 38, since its +16 final margin (57–41) was narrower in the September poll (55–42).

I'm reconsidering the bond angle: voters often turn against bonds when debt is the focus, and I'm recalling that the March 2020 school bond, Prop 13, failed despite majority support.

I'm trying to pin down whether Prop 13 from March 2020, a school facilities bond, actually failed, since the sources I'm recalling disagree on its vote share and on whether the 55% threshold applied. My sense is that it fell short, which would matter for how I think about bond measures in general.

I'm going back over whether Prop 13 from March 2020 actually failed, since I'm unsure whether the 55% threshold applied and what its final yes share was. I'm also thinking the PPIC note on it might be a side detail rather than something that changes the picture for this measure.

I'm weighing whether the Yes side's support erodes in the final days, since opposition spending usually drives that. Here the No side has little money, though it has earned media and newspaper endorsements, which can still matter in low-information races. Emotional Yes ads may hold up better than the more technical No critiques, and I'm checking whether party endorsements on either side change that.

I'm weighing the Republican Party's endorsement, which may not move Republican voters much. Still, the measure has broad majority support across partisan and demographic groups, which looks like a strong sign. Against that, the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association is opposing it with anti-bond messaging that could persuade conservatives, though Republicans are only about a quarter of likely voters.

I'm checking whether any lawsuit has been filed to pull Prop 38 from the ballot, since a court removal would change the answer entirely. An initiative can't be withdrawn once it qualifies, and challenges like this usually come before the ballot pamphlet is printed, so removal seems unlikely.

I'm now thinking about whether to look up Ballotpedia's page for Prop 38, which might have a polling section and more support data. I'll also check whether any late news or spending figures for the measure are worth noting.

I'm planning to check Ballotpedia's page for Prop 38, since it may list the support and opposition data I need. They’d take out debt to pay for housing and medical research. Follow the election results in California: Sign up for our newsletter (https://calmatters.org/subscribe-to-calmatters/california-election-newsletter/) to receive alerts when the contests for governor, Prop. 40, insurance commissioner and other key results are called. Your November ballot is welcoming you to make it rain … in bonds. You’ll see an El Nino-sized set of propositions that could flood the housing construction and science research components of the California economy with $44 billion of bond spending if the measures pass. Two of those bond proposals — Proposition 1 (https://calmatters.org/housing/homelessness/2026/10/prop-1-housing-bond/) for housing and Proposition 38 (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/10/prop-38-california/) for immunology research — are the traditional borrow-now, pay-back-later arrangements that add a few billion dollars to the overall cost of the propositions. A third, Proposition 37 (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/prop-37-explained-homeownership/), is an atypical measure that amounts to a low-risk radical experiment that taxpayers likely won’t be on the hook for, at least not directly. Historically, bond propositions win the approval of voters at higher rates than other measures. Since 2000, voters passed 23 of the 26 statewide bonds before them, an 88% yay rate. In recent years voters approved billions in bond debt for school construction, combatting the effects of climate change and housing for veterans. Bonds are a form of debt that the state must pay off over time, and that means annual payments with interest (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/voter-info/overview-state-bond-debt.htm). The state spends $6 billion annually to repay about $80 billion of bonds. Voters and lawmakers have also approved $40 billion in bonds that have yet to be sold. Fortunately for your ballot studying, the following cheat sheet is a primer on just the three bonds before you. Prop. 1: Affordable housing If voters say yes, Prop. 1 would permit California’s treasurer (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-1-housing-bond/) to sell $11.25 billion in general obligation bonds. That money would provide various types of housing, including to veterans, homeless Californians, renters, homeowners, farmworkers, students and tribes. The measure dedicates $7 billion to constructing, refurbishing, or acquiring apartment complexes, primarily through loans to developers of affordable housing. These developments must serve low-income residents, reserving at least 10% of units for extremely low-income households. Over $1 billion of this total supports permanent and interim housing for the homeless. The bond, if passed, would result in some 40,000 new rental units, wrote (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop1-110326.pdf) the Legislative Analyst’s Office, which is the nonpartisan think-tank of the Legislature. This is the only bond measure on the ballot put forward by lawmakers. The other two secured enough signatures from voters to secure a spot for the November election. Opposition to this bond is minimal. The state Republican Party’s officially neutral on the measure. Several Republican lawmakers in June voted no on the bill that metamorphosed into this bond. They argued that the bill’s title — The Veterans and Affordable Housing Bond Act (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/bills/ca_202520260sb417) — misled the public on just how much of the bond revenue would support veterans. The answer? $1.25 billion for veterans to secure home loans. Another $350 million would head to the state’s two public university systems to help finance the development of student dorms. But with costs per bed often exceeding $250,000, all those tens of millions of dollars would secure dorms for around 1,300 students. Read CalMatters’ Marisa Kendall’s guide to Prop. 1 (https://calmatters.org/housing/homelessness/2026/10/prop-1-housing-bond/). Prop. 37: Help for down payments This bond measure is strange (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-37-homebuyers-loan/), novel and introduces a bevy of unknowns. Confused? So is everyone else, which is why CalMatters’ housing reporter Ben Christopher described this unorthodox proposition as “plainly weird.” (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/prop-37-explained-homeownership/) Prop. 37 should be viewed as a way to help buyers of new homes secure down payments. The language permits individuals to apply for as much as 17% of the purchase price of a new house, condo or townhome. That covers much of the typical 20% down payment. Who’s eligible? Roughly 90% of all California renters. The income caps vary by county, so around $115,000 in Imperial and north of $400,000 in San Mateo for a family of three. Eligible homes must satisfy several conditions: They’re new or newly converted and don’t cost more than roughly $1.5 million in the Bay Area or $1 million in Riverside — again, it’s based on a weedy formula by county. What won’t it do? Add to the state’s debt repayment log. This is not a bond that taxpayers will pay back; instead private lenders who provide this bond money will be repaid by homebuyers in the form of interest payments. How many homes this could buy is impossible to predict. That number depends on how much the new homes cost, the incomes of the homebuyers and whether developers build new homes. Most renters today couldn’t afford even the cheapest new homes, said Eric McGhee, an analyst for the nonprofit Public Policy Institute of California who’s written about Prop. 37 (https://www.ppic.org/blog/how-many-might-actually-use-the-down-payment-assistance-in-proposition-37/). He estimated that anywhere from 60,000 to more than 1.8 million buyers could take advantage of the down payment assistance through this bond measure. The lower end assumes a 20% down payment on the most expensive homes. The higher end assumes 5% down payments on the least expensive homes. Prop. 38: Immunology research This bond proposal (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-38-research-bond/) would commit $4.2 billion to a single, unnamed nonprofit institute that focuses on immunology research and cures for major diseases such as Alzheimer’s, cancer and heart disease. The same amount would be distributed to a committee that’d identify a limited number of researchers at public universities and nonprofits who study immunology and immunotherapies. Previous reporting by CalMatters (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/07/proposition-38-california/) found only one institute in California currently meets Prop. 38’s criteria for half of the money: the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy. The institute’s primary funder is billionaire Gary K. Michelson, who wrote Prop. 38 and is by far the largest donor to its political campaign. Additional CalMatters reporting raises the question of how ready is the institute to implement the bond’s vast dollars. The institute had only three employees (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/10/prop-38-california/) as of last month, far fewer than the 51 it planned to have on staff last year. The Yes on 38 campaign says the bond revenue is needed to hedge against the Trump administration’s ongoing efforts to cut federal science research or limit what’s studied. They argue that any curtailment of drug trials and other therapies can lead to avoidable pain and death for patients of debilitating maladies. Opponents of the measure fault it for concentrating half the money in a single institute and limiting which other researchers can receive the funding. They say science research is best performed in a competitive environment that’s open to all of California’s nonprofit and public university scientists. I'm noting that CalMatters puts the historical approval rate for statewide bonds at 88%, with 23 of 26 passing since 2000. That makes bonds look strong on a base rate. But I'm also thinking the record includes plenty that passed by wide margins, and Prop 14 in 2020 squeaked by at 51%, so the base rate may hide closer calls.

I'm checking which bonds failed, since the 88% figure means only a few did. I'm also weighing whether citizen-initiated bonds fare differently from legislative ones, and I'm trying to recall a few examples I'm not certain about.

I'm now going through which statewide bonds passed in recent years, weighing the 2016 school bond and the 2018 housing and homelessness measures against the narrow 2020 Prop 14 win. I'm also still unsure whether the March 2020 Prop 13 failure is right, since I can't firmly recall its vote share.

I'm trying to pin down whether the March 2020 Prop 13 failed, since I can't firmly recall its vote share and the 55% figure doesn't square with it failing. That detail is a tangent, though, so I'd rather not lean on it. The main point stands: bond measures have passed at a high rate historically.

I'm weighing whether the Yes side's funding edge, the steady PPIC numbers, and the lack of organized opposition push the odds well past even, and I'm putting the chance of passage somewhere around 75 to 85 percent. I'm also thinking about the "billionaire self-dealing" framing and the HJTA's anti-tax campaign as the main risks, and I want to check whether any fresh polls from early November shifted the picture.

I'm planning to check for any fresh polls on Prop 38 from pollsters like POLITICO or Target Point, searching for the measure's name and a November 2026 date.

assistantMessageEvent.content:
I'm looking at the On Point Politics forecast from Nov 2, 2026, which projects Yes at 58.1% with a 94.8% chance of passing. It's a model blending comparable measures and polls, with polls pulled toward the forecast by recency and size after undecided voters are split two to one for No. The 80% range runs from 51.8% to 64.3%, and I'm working out what spread the probability implies.

I'm checking whether the forecast's 94.8% is too confident, since ballot measure polls often miss by 5 to 10 points. Working from its 80% range, the implied spread is about 4.9 points, and with a wider error of 6 to 8 points my estimate of Yes passing lands around 80 to 88%. That's below the forecast's figure, but the direction is the same: Yes is more likely to win.

Next I'm checking the wording of the question against the page: "Which side is more likely to win?" most plausibly means the Yes side, since the page is the Yes/No measure, so a "yes" answer lines up with the forecast. I also want to confirm the timing, since the page was updated Nov 2 with the vote a day away, meaning this is a forecast and not a result.

I'm weighing the risks against the forecast: the final PPIC poll shows Yes at 57–41 with 2% undecided and a steady trend, but the No side has a huge funding edge, opposition from most editorial boards, and a mix of endorsements on both sides. Historically about 88% of statewide bonds since 2000 have passed, which supports a Yes lean.

I'm weighing the counterpoints: Prop 14 and Prop 1 both passed only narrowly, and the earmark and "billionaire" framing could erode support in the final days. Heavy early voting also means a good share of the tally is already locked in, from ballots cast when Yes was likely around 55–57%.

I'm weighing whether the PPIC final poll numbers shift the picture, and I'm noting that the On Point model's 2:1 undecided split only moves Yes by a fraction of a point, since undecideds are just 2%. I'm also thinking about checking how PPIC's final initiative polls have matched actual results over past cycles, so I can judge how much to trust a poll-based lean.

I'm pulling up the PPIC final polls from 2024 to see how their October numbers compared with the actual results. A few measures gained for Yes after the poll, others held steady, and one, the $18 minimum wage measure, slipped and failed. That's a useful check on how much a late poll lead can move.

I'm going back over how PPIC's October polls for popular measures compared with final results in 2024, where most came within about 5 points of the final yes share. Billionaire Gary Michelson Backs $8.4 Billion Research Bond and Pledges $120 Million
Andre Savage (https://www.briefs.co/author/andre/)
Published Oct 21, 2026
Share:
Summary:
Gary Michelson has committed $120 million to launch a Los Angeles immunology institute and is pushing Proposition 38 to supercharge state funding for the field.
Proposition 38 seeks $8.4 billion in state bonds for immune system research and therapies for cancer, heart disease and Alzheimer's, with a Nov. 3 vote among 14 statewide measures.
No new tax is proposed. Debt service would come from California's general fund, which also covers schools, health care and other services, with $500 million to $600 million a year projected for about 20 years.
The pitch and the institute
Gary Michelson, a 77-year-old former spine surgeon and prolific inventor, has put $120 million on the table to help build the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy in Los Angeles. He co-founded and chairs the institute, which was formed in 2024, and says the public bond is meant to keep U.S. science moving as the Trump administration reduces federal research dollars.
He is not alone in bankrolling the project. Michelson and his wife, Alya, join co-founders committing a combined $250 million, among them financier Michael Milken and Facebook's first president, Sean Parker. The institute is slated to take space in a redeveloped former mall that UCLA is turning into a research park.
Michelson frames the bet as a public choice. "California's initiative system was created so that the voters could bypass the politicians and decide important priorities directly," he wrote. "There is no more important priority than preventing and curing fatal diseases. We trust the people of California with this decision." He also said, "I won't make a single dollar from Prop 38, quite the opposite," adding that he backs the measure to give "millions of others a chance to live longer, healthier lives."

What Prop 38 would do
Prop 38 would raise $8.4 billion through state bonds to fund immunology, which studies how the body defends itself, and immunotherapy, which uses that system to fight disease. The target list includes cancer, heart disease and Alzheimer's. Voters will decide on Nov. 3, with the measure one of 14 on the ballot.
There is no new tax in the proposal. Instead, the state would make payments from the general fund that also supports K-12 education, health care and other public programs. California's Legislative Analyst's Office estimates $500 million to $600 million a year in payments for about two decades. The measure requires that 10% of any revenue from funded discoveries flow back to the state to help cover principal and interest, though the analyst cautions that such income is uncertain and may take years or decades to arrive.
Who could get the money, and who is for and against
The statute does not name Michelson's institute. Even so, the eligibility rules - covering facilities, philanthropic support, and links with a University of California medical center - seem to exclude any other in-state institute, according to a CalMatters review. The Proposition 38 campaign argues the requirements are meant to anchor a world-class hub with the people, tools and clinical access to speed breakthroughs. The California Department of Public Health would make the final award.
Governor Gavin Newsom endorsed the bond this month, calling it a way to support lifesaving work and offset federal pullbacks. UCLA has been among the universities the Trump administration has targeted over allegations of antisemitism and discrimination. Michelson says the state effort would help sustain American research leadership amid those cuts.

Not everyone is on board with the financing model. Stanford School of Medicine senior scholar Robert Kaplan, who previously served as an associate director at the National Institutes of Health, warns that "Taxpayers take all the financial risk," describing the approach as "putting all your eggs in one basket." He estimates therapies would need to generate about $120 billion in intellectual property to pay back an $8.4 billion bond if the state is recouping 10% of revenue, and he argues the plan could channel "perhaps $100 billion in intellectual property revenue to a small organization that's a creation of billionaires."
Kaplan points to California's earlier stem cell bond program, approved in 2004, which he says has returned roughly $16 million in royalties, less than 1% of the combined principal and interest. He also notes the new debt would land as other state services, including health care, contend with federal reductions.
Money, momentum and the market angle
State disclosure records show the Yes on 38 campaign has taken in $72 million, with $66.2 million contributed by Michelson. The No on 38 side reported around $9,000. In polling last month from the Public Policy Institute of California, 55% of likely voters supported the measure. The same survey found 52% backed a separate one-time 5% tax on billionaire (https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-10-21/billionaire-asks-californians-to-bankroll-disease-prevention-lab) wealth, largely for health care, while much of the campaign spotlight has centered on Proposition 40, the wealth tax (https://www.briefs.co/news/billionaires-are-fleeing-californias-proposed-wealth-tax-for-nevada/) question.
Support also comes from researchers squeezed by federal cutbacks. Jillian McCool lost a postdoctoral role in immunology and biology at Lawrence Livermore Laboratory after her grant was cut last year. Now studying bees at the University of California at Davis, she put it bluntly: "I hate billionaires, but if you want to spend money on science I'll take it."
In plain English: the financial payoff depends on whether public science turns into products. The measure directs 10% of resulting revenue to the state, but timelines are long and outcomes uncertain. Still, the broader field is moving. The 2025 Nobel Prize in medicine honored three scientists who identified regulatory T cells, the immune system's internal security team that stops it from attacking the body's own tissues.
The bottom line for your portfolio is about cash flows and concentration risk. If Prop 38 passes, California's general fund would shoulder $500 million to $600 million a year for about 20 years, with potential upside from licensing if big therapies emerge. The design effectively concentrates a large bet in a single qualifying center, increasing the chance of a coordinated research hub while focusing both risk and reward. Michelson says the institute will proceed even if voters say no. He has signed the Giving Pledge and maintains he will not personally profit from the measure.

Billionaire Gary Michelson Backs $8.4 Billion Research Bond and Pledges $120 Million
Andre Savage (https://www.briefs.co/author/andre/)
Published Oct 21, 2026
Share:
Summary:
Gary Michelson has committed $120 million to launch a Los Angeles immunology institute and is pushing Proposition 38 to supercharge state funding for the field.
Proposition 38 seeks $8.4 billion in state bonds for immune system research and therapies for cancer, heart disease and Alzheimer's, with a Nov. 3 vote among 14 statewide measures.
No new tax is proposed. Debt service would come from California's general fund, which also covers schools, health care and other services, with $500 million to $600 million a year projected for about 20 years.
The pitch and the institute
Gary Michelson, a 77-year-old former spine surgeon and prolific inventor, has put $120 million on the table to help build the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy in Los Angeles. He co-founded and chairs the institute, which was formed in 2024, and says the public bond is meant to keep U.S. science moving as the Trump administration reduces federal research dollars.
He is not alone in bankrolling the project. Michelson and his wife, Alya, join co-founders committing a combined $250 million, among them financier Michael Milken and Facebook's first president, Sean Parker. The institute is slated to take space in a redeveloped former mall that UCLA is turning into a research park.
Michelson frames the bet as a public choice. "California's initiative system was created so that the voters could bypass the politicians and decide important priorities directly," he wrote. "There is no more important priority than preventing and curing fatal diseases. We trust the people of California with this decision." He also said, "I won't make a single dollar from Prop 38, quite the opposite," adding that he backs the measure to give "millions of others a chance to live longer, healthier lives."

What Prop 38 would do
Prop 38 would raise $8.4 billion through state bonds to fund immunology, which studies how the body defends itself, and immunotherapy, which uses that system to fight disease. The target list includes cancer, heart disease and Alzheimer's. Voters will decide on Nov. 3, with the measure one of 14 on the ballot.
There is no new tax in the proposal. Instead, the state would make payments from the general fund that also supports K-12 education, health care and other public programs. California's Legislative Analyst's Office estimates $500 million to $600 million a year in payments for about two decades. The measure requires that 10% of any revenue from funded discoveries flow back to the state to help cover principal and interest, though the analyst cautions that such income is uncertain and may take years or decades to arrive.
Who could get the money, and who is for and against
The statute does not name Michelson's institute. Even so, the eligibility rules - covering facilities, philanthropic support, and links with a University of California medical center - seem to exclude any other in-state institute, according to a CalMatters review. The Proposition 38 campaign argues the requirements are meant to anchor a world-class hub with the people, tools and clinical access to speed breakthroughs. The California Department of Public Health would make the final award.
Governor Gavin Newsom endorsed the bond this month, calling it a way to support lifesaving work and offset federal pullbacks. UCLA has been among the universities the Trump administration has targeted over allegations of antisemitism and discrimination. Michelson says the state effort would help sustain American research leadership amid those cuts.

Not everyone is on board with the financing model. Stanford School of Medicine senior scholar Robert Kaplan, who previously served as an associate director at the National Institutes of Health, warns that "Taxpayers take all the financial risk," describing the approach as "putting all your eggs in one basket." He estimates therapies would need to generate about $120 billion in intellectual property to pay back an $8.4 billion bond if the state is recouping 10% of revenue, and he argues the plan could channel "perhaps $100 billion in intellectual property revenue to a small organization that's a creation of billionaires."
Kaplan points to California's earlier stem cell bond program, approved in 2004, which he says has returned roughly $16 million in royalties, less than 1% of the combined principal and interest. He also notes the new debt would land as other state services, including health care, contend with federal reductions.
Money, momentum and the market angle
State disclosure records show the Yes on 38 campaign has taken in $72 million, with $66.2 million contributed by Michelson. The No on 38 side reported around $9,000. In polling last month from the Public Policy Institute of California, 55% of likely voters supported the measure. The same survey found 52% backed a separate one-time 5% tax on billionaire (https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-10-21/billionaire-asks-californians-to-bankroll-disease-prevention-lab) wealth, largely for health care, while much of the campaign spotlight has centered on Proposition 40, the wealth tax (https://www.briefs.co/news/billionaires-are-fleeing-californias-proposed-wealth-tax-for-nevada/) question.
Support also comes from researchers squeezed by federal cutbacks. Jillian McCool lost a postdoctoral role in immunology and biology at Lawrence Livermore Laboratory after her grant was cut last year. Now studying bees at the University of California at Davis, she put it bluntly: "I hate billionaires, but if you want to spend money on science I'll take it."
In plain English: the financial payoff depends on whether public science turns into products. The measure directs 10% of resulting revenue to the state, but timelines are long and outcomes uncertain. Still, the broader field is moving. The 2025 Nobel Prize in medicine honored three scientists who identified regulatory T cells, the immune system's internal security team that stops it from attacking the body's own tissues.
The bottom line for your portfolio is about cash flows and concentration risk. If Prop 38 passes, California's general fund would shoulder $500 million to $600 million a year for about 20 years, with potential upside from licensing if big therapies emerge. The design effectively concentrates a large bet in a single qualifying center, increasing the chance of a coordinated research hub while focusing both risk and reward. Michelson says the institute will proceed even if voters say no. He has signed the Giving Pledge and maintains he will not personally profit from the measure.

Billionaire Gary Michelson Backs $8.4 Billion Research Bond and Pledges $120 Million
Andre Savage (https://www.briefs.co/author/andre/)
Published Oct 21, 2026
Share:
Summary:
Gary Michelson has committed $120 million to launch a Los Angeles immunology institute and is pushing Proposition 38 to supercharge state funding for the field.
Proposition 38 seeks $8.4 billion in state bonds for immune system research and therapies for cancer, heart disease and Alzheimer's, with a Nov. 3 vote among 14 statewide measures.
No new tax is proposed. Debt service would come from California's general fund, which also covers schools, health care and other services, with $500 million to $600 million a year projected for about 20 years.
The pitch and the institute
Gary Michelson, a 77-year-old former spine surgeon and prolific inventor, has put $120 million on the table to help build the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy in Los Angeles. He co-founded and chairs the institute, which was formed in 2024, and says the public bond is meant to keep U.S. science moving as the Trump administration reduces federal research dollars.
He is not alone in bankrolling the project. Michelson and his wife, Alya, join co-founders committing a combined $250 million, among them financier Michael Milken and Facebook's first president, Sean Parker. The institute is slated to take space in a redeveloped former mall that UCLA is turning into a research park.
Michelson frames the bet as a public choice. "California's initiative system was created so that the voters could bypass the politicians and decide important priorities directly," he wrote. "There is no more important priority than preventing and curing fatal diseases. We trust the people of California with this decision." He also said, "I won't make a single dollar from Prop 38, quite the opposite," adding that he backs the measure to give "millions of others a chance to live longer, healthier lives."

What Prop 38 would do
Prop 38 would raise $8.4 billion through state bonds to fund immunology, which studies how the body defends itself, and immunotherapy, which uses that system to fight disease. The target list includes cancer, heart disease and Alzheimer's. Voters will decide on Nov. 3, with the measure one of 14 on the ballot.
There is no new tax in the proposal. Instead, the state would make payments from the general fund that also supports K-12 education, health care and other public programs. California's Legislative Analyst's Office estimates $500 million to $600 million a year in payments for about two decades. The measure requires that 10% of any revenue from funded discoveries flow back to the state to help cover principal and interest, though the analyst cautions that such income is uncertain and may take years or decades to arrive.
Who could get the money, and who is for and against
The statute does not name Michelson's institute. Even so, the eligibility rules - covering facilities, philanthropic support, and links with a University of California medical center - seem to exclude any other in-state institute, according to a CalMatters review. The Proposition 38 campaign argues the requirements are meant to anchor a world-class hub with the people, tools and clinical access to speed breakthroughs. The California Department of Public Health would make the final award.
Governor Gavin Newsom endorsed the bond this month, calling it a way to support lifesaving work and offset federal pullbacks. UCLA has been among the universities the Trump administration has targeted over allegations of antisemitism and discrimination. Michelson says the state effort would help sustain American research leadership amid those cuts.

Not everyone is on board with the financing model. Stanford School of Medicine senior scholar Robert Kaplan, who previously served as an associate director at the National Institutes of Health, warns that "Taxpayers take all the financial risk," describing the approach as "putting all your eggs in one basket." He estimates therapies would need to generate about $120 billion in intellectual property to pay back an $8.4 billion bond if the state is recouping 10% of revenue, and he argues the plan could channel "perhaps $100 billion in intellectual property revenue to a small organization that's a creation of billionaires."
Kaplan points to California's earlier stem cell bond program, approved in 2004, which he says has returned roughly $16 million in royalties, less than 1% of the combined principal and interest. He also notes the new debt would land as other state services, including health care, contend with federal reductions.
Money, momentum and the market angle
State disclosure records show the Yes on 38 campaign has taken in $72 million, with $66.2 million contributed by Michelson. The No on 38 side reported around $9,000. In polling last month from the Public Policy Institute of California, 55% of likely voters supported the measure. The same survey found 52% backed a separate one-time 5% tax on billionaire (https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-10-21/billionaire-asks-californians-to-bankroll-disease-prevention-lab) wealth, largely for health care, while much of the campaign spotlight has centered on Proposition 40, the wealth tax (https://www.briefs.co/news/billionaires-are-fleeing-californias-proposed-wealth-tax-for-nevada/) question.
Support also comes from researchers squeezed by federal cutbacks. Jillian McCool lost a postdoctoral role in immunology and biology at Lawrence Livermore Laboratory after her grant was cut last year. Now studying bees at the University of California at Davis, she put it bluntly: "I hate billionaires, but if you want to spend money on science I'll take it."
In plain English: the financial payoff depends on whether public science turns into products. The measure directs 10% of resulting revenue to the state, but timelines are long and outcomes uncertain. Still, the broader field is moving. The 2025 Nobel Prize in medicine honored three scientists who identified regulatory T cells, the immune system's internal security team that stops it from attacking the body's own tissues.
The bottom line for your portfolio is about cash flows and concentration risk. If Prop 38 passes, California's general fund would shoulder $500 million to $600 million a year for about 20 years, with potential upside from licensing if big therapies emerge. The design effectively concentrates a large bet in a single qualifying center, increasing the chance of a coordinated research hub while focusing both risk and reward. Michelson says the institute will proceed even if voters say no. He has signed the Giving Pledge and maintains he will not personally profit from the measure.

I'm looking at the On Point Politics forecast from Nov 2, 2026, which projects Yes at 58.1% with a 94.8% chance of passing. It's a model blending comparable measures and polls, with polls pulled toward the forecast by recency and size after undecided voters are split two to one for No. The 80% range runs from 51.8% to 64.3%, and I'm working out what spread the probability implies.

I'm checking whether the forecast's 94.8% is too confident, since ballot measure polls often miss by 5 to 10 points. Working from its 80% range, the implied spread is about 4.9 points, and with a wider error of 6 to 8 points my estimate of Yes passing lands around 80 to 88%. That's below the forecast's figure, but the direction is the same: Yes is more likely to win.

Next I'm checking the wording of the question against the page: "Which side is more likely to win?" most plausibly means the Yes side, since the page is the Yes/No measure, so a "yes" answer lines up with the forecast. I also want to confirm the timing, since the page was updated Nov 2 with the vote a day away, meaning this is a forecast and not a result.

I'm weighing the risks against the forecast: the final PPIC poll shows Yes at 57–41 with 2% undecided and a steady trend, but the No side has a huge funding edge, opposition from most editorial boards, and a mix of endorsements on both sides. Historically about 88% of statewide bonds since 2000 have passed, which supports a Yes lean.

I'm weighing the counterpoints: Prop 14 and Prop 1 both passed only narrowly, and the earmark and "billionaire" framing could erode support in the final days. Heavy early voting also means a good share of the tally is already locked in, from ballots cast when Yes was likely around 55–57%.

I'm weighing whether the PPIC final poll numbers shift the picture, and I'm noting that the On Point model's 2:1 undecided split only moves Yes by a fraction of a point, since undecideds are just 2%. I'm also thinking about checking how PPIC's final initiative polls have matched actual results over past cycles, so I can judge how much to trust a poll-based lean.

Billionaire Gary Michelson Backs $8.4 Billion Research Bond and Pledges $120 Million
Andre Savage (https://www.briefs.co/author/andre/)
Published Oct 21, 2026
Share:
Summary:
Gary Michelson has committed $120 million to launch a Los Angeles immunology institute and is pushing Proposition 38 to supercharge state funding for the field.
Proposition 38 seeks $8.4 billion in state bonds for immune system research and therapies for cancer, heart disease and Alzheimer's, with a Nov. 3 vote among 14 statewide measures.
No new tax is proposed. Debt service would come from California's general fund, which also covers schools, health care and other services, with $500 million to $600 million a year projected for about 20 years.
The pitch and the institute
Gary Michelson, a 77-year-old former spine surgeon and prolific inventor, has put $120 million on the table to help build the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy in Los Angeles. He co-founded and chairs the institute, which was formed in 2024, and says the public bond is meant to keep U.S. science moving as the Trump administration reduces federal research dollars.
He is not alone in bankrolling the project. Michelson and his wife, Alya, join co-founders committing a combined $250 million, among them financier Michael Milken and Facebook's first president, Sean Parker. The institute is slated to take space in a redeveloped former mall that UCLA is turning into a research park.
Michelson frames the bet as a public choice. "California's initiative system was created so that the voters could bypass the politicians and decide important priorities directly," he wrote. "There is no more important priority than preventing and curing fatal diseases. We trust the people of California with this decision." He also said, "I won't make a single dollar from Prop 38, quite the opposite," adding that he backs the measure to give "millions of others a chance to live longer, healthier lives."

What Prop 38 would do
Prop 38 would raise $8.4 billion through state bonds to fund immunology, which studies how the body defends itself, and immunotherapy, which uses that system to fight disease. The target list includes cancer, heart disease and Alzheimer's. Voters will decide on Nov. 3, with the measure one of 14 on the ballot.
There is no new tax in the proposal. Instead, the state would make payments from the general fund that also supports K-12 education, health care and other public programs. California's Legislative Analyst's Office estimates $500 million to $600 million a year in payments for about two decades. The measure requires that 10% of any revenue from funded discoveries flow back to the state to help cover principal and interest, though the analyst cautions that such income is uncertain and may take years or decades to arrive.
Who could get the money, and who is for and against
The statute does not name Michelson's institute. Even so, the eligibility rules - covering facilities, philanthropic support, and links with a University of California medical center - seem to exclude any other in-state institute, according to a CalMatters review. The Proposition 38 campaign argues the requirements are meant to anchor a world-class hub with the people, tools and clinical access to speed breakthroughs. The California Department of Public Health would make the final award.
Governor Gavin Newsom endorsed the bond this month, calling it a way to support lifesaving work and offset federal pullbacks. UCLA has been among the universities the Trump administration has targeted over allegations of antisemitism and discrimination. Michelson says the state effort would help sustain American research leadership amid those cuts.

Not everyone is on board with the financing model. Stanford School of Medicine senior scholar Robert Kaplan, who previously served as an associate director at the National Institutes of Health, warns that "Taxpayers take all the financial risk," describing the approach as "putting all your eggs in one basket." He estimates therapies would need to generate about $120 billion in intellectual property to pay back an $8.4 billion bond if the state is recouping 10% of revenue, and he argues the plan could channel "perhaps $100 billion in intellectual property revenue to a small organization that's a creation of billionaires."
Kaplan points to California's earlier stem cell bond program, approved in 2004, which he says has returned roughly $16 million in royalties, less than 1% of the combined principal and interest. He also notes the new debt would land as other state services, including health care, contend with federal reductions.
Money, momentum and the market angle
State disclosure records show the Yes on 38 campaign has taken in $72 million, with $66.2 million contributed by Michelson. The No on 38 side reported around $9,000. In polling last month from the Public Policy Institute of California, 55% of likely voters supported the measure. The same survey found 52% backed a separate one-time 5% tax on billionaire (https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-10-21/billionaire-asks-californians-to-bankroll-disease-prevention-lab) wealth, largely for health care, while much of the campaign spotlight has centered on Proposition 40, the wealth tax (https://www.briefs.co/news/billionaires-are-fleeing-californias-proposed-wealth-tax-for-nevada/) question.
Support also comes from researchers squeezed by federal cutbacks. Jillian McCool lost a postdoctoral role in immunology and biology at Lawrence Livermore Laboratory after her grant was cut last year. Now studying bees at the University of California at Davis, she put it bluntly: "I hate billionaires, but if you want to spend money on science I'll take it."
In plain English: the financial payoff depends on whether public science turns into products. The measure directs 10% of resulting revenue to the state, but timelines are long and outcomes uncertain. Still, the broader field is moving. The 2025 Nobel Prize in medicine honored three scientists who identified regulatory T cells, the immune system's internal security team that stops it from attacking the body's own tissues.
The bottom line for your portfolio is about cash flows and concentration risk. If Prop 38 passes, California's general fund would shoulder $500 million to $600 million a year for about 20 years, with potential upside from licensing if big therapies emerge. The design effectively concentrates a large bet in a single qualifying center, increasing the chance of a coordinated research hub while focusing both risk and reward. Michelson says the institute will proceed even if voters say no. He has signed the Giving Pledge and maintains he will not personally profit from the measure.

Stanford School of Medicine senior scholar Robert Kaplan, who previously served as an associate director at the National Institutes of Health, warns that "Taxpayers take all the financial risk," describing the approach as "putting all your eggs in one basket." He estimates therapies would need to generate about $120 billion in intellectual property to pay back an $8.4 billion bond if the state is recouping 10% of revenue, and he argues the plan could channel "perhaps $100 billion in intellectual property revenue to a small organization that's a creation of billionaires."
Kaplan points to California's earlier stem cell bond program, approved in 2004, which he says has returned roughly $16 million in royalties, less than 1% of the combined principal and interest. He also notes the new debt would land as other state services, including health care, contend with federal reductions.
Money, momentum and the market angle
State disclosure records show the Yes on 38 campaign has taken in $72 million, with $66.2 million contributed by Michelson. The No on 38 side reported around $9,000. In polling last month from the Public Policy Institute of California, 55% of likely voters supported the measure. The same survey found 52% backed a separate one-time 5% tax on billionaire (https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-10-21/billionaire-asks-californians-to-bankroll-disease-prevention-lab) wealth, largely for health care, while much of the campaign spotlight has centered on Proposition 40, the wealth tax (https://www.briefs.co/news/billionaires-are-fleeing-californias-proposed-wealth-tax-for-nevada/) question.
Support also comes from researchers squeezed by federal cutbacks. Jillian McCool lost a postdoctoral role in immunology and biology at Lawrence Livermore Laboratory after her grant was cut last year. Now studying bees at the University of California at Davis, she put it bluntly: "I hate billionaires, but if you want to spend money on science I'll take it."
In plain English: the financial payoff depends on whether public science turns into products. The measure directs 10% of resulting revenue to the state, but timelines are long and outcomes uncertain. Still, the broader field is moving. The 2025 Nobel Prize in medicine honored three scientists who identified regulatory T cells, the immune system's internal security team that stops it from attacking the body's own tissues.
The bottom line for your portfolio is about cash flows and concentration risk. If Prop 38 passes, California's general fund would shoulder $500 million to $600 million a year for about 20 years, with potential upside from licensing if big therapies emerge. The design effectively concentrates a large bet in a single qualifying center, increasing the chance of a coordinated research hub while focusing both risk and reward. Michelson says the institute will proceed even if voters say no. He has signed the Giving Pledge and maintains he will not personally profit from the measure.
